Other members: ~brennen~/~brannte~, ~kennen~/~kannte~, ~nennen~/~nannte~, ~rennen~/~rannte~, ~senden~/~sandte~, ~wenden~/~wandte~. ~Denken~ also shares with ~bringen~ (~brachte~) an additional consonant change in the past (the ~k~ before the dental suffix became ~ch~ by an early Germanic process); some linguists therefore interpret ~bringen~'s vowel change as a true ablaut grade shift rather than the umlaut removal seen in ~denken~ (see ~brennen~ for the underlying Rückumlaut mechanism). The same PIE root yields ~Dank~ ("thanks") and ~Gedanke~ ("thought"), reflecting the deep semantic connection between thinking and thanking in the Germanic languages. Cognate with Bavarian ~denkn~, Dutch ~denken~, Low German ~denken~, West Frisian ~tinke~, English ~think~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
en.derben: Not an independent verb of modern German; it survives only inside ~verderben~ ("to spoil, ruin, perish"). From MHG ~derben~ ("to perish"), from Proto-West Germanic *~derban~, from Proto-Germanic *~derbaną~ ("to work; to perish"), from PIE *~dʰerHbʰ-~ ("to labor, perish"), cognate with Lithuanian ~dirbti~ ("to work"). A class III strong verb, and the compound keeps the class III ablaut intact: ~verderben~, ~verdarb~, ~verdorben~, the same series as ~sterben~ and ~werfen~. Cognate with Old English ~deorfan~ ("to toil, be in peril, perish") and Middle English ~derven~; the adjective ~derb~ ("coarse, blunt") is a relative by way of Proto-Germanic *~derbaz~, as is Old Norse ~djarfr~ ("bold").
en.deuten:
From Middle High German ~diuten~, from Old High German ~diuten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiudijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þiudijaną~ ("to associate with; to interpret; to point out"), derived from Proto-Germanic *~þeudō~ ("people"), from PIE *~tewtéh₂~ ("people"). Cognate with Dutch ~duiden~ ("to indicate, to interpret"), Icelandic ~þýða~ ("to translate"), Swedish ~tyda~ ("to interpret, to decipher"), Danish ~tyde~ ("to interpret").

The semantic path from "people" to "interpret" is one of the most fascinating in Germanic etymology. The original meaning was "to make intelligible to the people" — to translate from learned or sacred language into the common tongue. This is precisely the same word that gives German ~deutsch~ ("German"), literally "of the people," via Proto-Germanic *~þiudiskaz~ ("pertaining to the people"), which distinguished the vernacular Germanic languages from Latin. To ~deuten~ was, in a sense, to speak ~deutsch~ — to render comprehensible in the people's language. The modern meanings — "to interpret" (dreams, omens, texts: ~Träume deuten~) and "to point" (~auf etwas deuten~, "to point at something") — both descend from this original act of making meaning accessible. The derived noun ~Bedeutung~ ("meaning, significance") and the adjective ~deutlich~ ("clear, distinct") preserve the interpretive core. That ~deutsch~ and ~deuten~ share a root is not mere folk etymology but genuine linguistic kinship: both spring from the Proto-Germanic concept of "the people" and their language.
en.dienen: From Middle High German ~dienen~, from Old High German ~dionōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þewanōną~ ("to serve"), a denominative verb derived from *~þewaz~ ("servant, slave"). The etymology of *~þewaz~ is uncertain; one hypothesis derives it from PIE *~tekʷ-~ ("to run"), with "servant" as "one who runs (errands)"; another connects it to *~tew(h₂)-~ ("to swell, grow"), though neither etymology is secure. The same Proto-Germanic root *~þewaz~ underlies Old English ~þegn~ ("thane, servant"), which by a remarkable social elevation came to mean "warrior, nobleman" and eventually became the Scottish title ~thane~ — immortalized in Shakespeare's ~Macbeth~. Cognate with Dutch ~dienen~, English ~thane~ (via the related noun), Danish ~tjene~.
en.dingen: From MHG ~dingen~ ("to negotiate, hire"), from OHG ~dingōn~ ("to hold court, negotiate"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þingōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þingōną~, a verb built on the noun *~þingą~ ("appointed time; assembly"), probably from PIE *~tenk-~ ("to be fitting, suitable"). Originally a weak verb: the strong forms ~dang~ and ~gedungen~ are a secondary acquisition that appears to have begun in Middle Low German, so modern German admits both ~dingte~/~gedingt~ and ~dang~/~gedungen~. Cognate with Dutch ~dingen~ ("to haggle, bid"), Danish ~tinge~, and — through the parent noun — English ~thing~ and Old Norse ~þing~. That noun is ~Ding~, which travelled from "assembly" to "the matter debated there" to "any object whatever," the same drift that left English with ~thing~ while Iceland kept its ~Alþingi~.
en.drehen:
From Middle High German ~dræjen~, ~dræhen~, from Old High German ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, twist, turn"). Cognate with Bavarian ~drahn~, Dutch ~draaien~, English ~throw~.

The cognate with English ~throw~ is not a false friend but a true one — it is simply that ~throw~ has shifted its meaning dramatically since the Old English period. Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist, turn," not "to hurl," and the act of hurling was expressed by the now-archaic ~weorpan~ (cognate with German ~werfen~). At some point in the Middle English period, ~throw~ displaced ~weorp-~ as the word for tossing and was itself displaced by ~warp~ as the word for twisting — a near-complete swap of semantic roles. The shared ancestry with ~drehen~ is visible in Dutch ~draaien~, Low German ~draien~. The PIE root *~terh₁-~ also underlies Latin ~terere~ ("to rub, wear away"), English ~thread~ (something twisted), and English ~throw~ (in the potters' sense: "to throw a pot" still means "to shape clay on a turning wheel").
en.dreschen: From MHG ~dreschen~, from OHG ~dreskan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þreskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þreskaną~, probably from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, turn"). A class III strong verb (~dreschen~, ~drosch~, ~gedroschen~). Cognate with English ~thresh~ and its doublet ~thrash~, Dutch ~dorsen~, Low German ~dörschen~, Danish ~tærske~, Swedish ~tröska~. Germanic threshing was done by treading the grain underfoot, and Romance borrowed the word in that sense: Italian ~trescare~ ("to caper, to dance") still stamps.
en.drießen: No longer an independent verb of modern German: ~drießen~ survives only inside ~verdrießen~ ("to annoy, vex") and its noun ~Verdruss~. From MHG ~driezen~, from OHG ~-driozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þreutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þreutaną~ ("to trouble, weary"), from PIE *~trewd-~ ("to push, press"). It was a class II strong verb, which is why the surviving compound still yields ~verdross~, ~verdrossen~. The same PIE root gives Latin ~trudere~ ("to thrust"), behind English ~intrude~ and ~extrude~, and Old English ~þrēotan~ ("to weary").
en.dringen:
From Middle High German ~dringen~, from Old High German ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). Akin to ~drängen~ ("to push, urge") and ~Drang~ ("urge, drive"). Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press, to crowd") and, more distantly, with English ~throng~.

~Dringen~ is a class III strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~. It means "to press through, to penetrate, to insist urgently." The related causative ~drängen~ ("to urge, to push") has the expected umlaut marking of Germanic causative formation: the base vowel ~a~ from the past tense grade becomes ~ä~ in the derived verb. The noun ~Drang~ ("drive, urge, impulse") is famous from the literary movement ~Sturm und Drang~ ("Storm and Drive"), the late 18th-century revolt against rationalist constraints that launched German Romanticism. English ~throng~ (a pressing crowd) preserves the original sense of people pressing together. The initial Proto-Germanic *~þr-~ cluster regularly became ~dr-~ in Old High German through the consonant shift.
en.drohen:
From Middle High German ~drōn~, ~drōwen~, from Old High German ~drouwen~, ~drōwen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrauwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þraujaną~ ("to threaten"). The archaic variant ~dräuen~ preserves the older vowel pattern more faithfully. Cognate with Old English ~þrēagan~ ("to rebuke, threaten"), Old Saxon ~thrōian~, Middle Dutch ~drouwen~.

The shift from ~drouwen~ to ~drohen~ involved a simplification of the diphthong ~ou~ to long ~ō~ and loss of the ~w~, a common phonological development in Middle High German. The older form ~dräuen~ (with umlaut from the ~j~ in *~þrauwijan~) survives in literary German and Luther's Bible translation but is otherwise archaic. The derived noun ~Drohung~ ("threat") and the compound ~bedrohen~ ("to threaten someone directly") are far more common in modern usage than the simplex ~drohen~ in isolation. English lost its cognate ~threaten~ (from ~þrēat~, a different formation) but the related Old English ~þrēagan~ ("to rebuke") died out, leaving no direct modern English reflex of this particular Germanic root.
en.drucken:
From Middle High German ~drucken~, from Old High German ~drucchen~/~drukken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~ ("to press"). This is a doublet of ~drücken~ ("to press, push"), which preserves the expected umlaut. The lack of umlaut in ~drucken~ reflects Upper German dialect phonology, where umlaut before a velar geminate was blocked. Since the first German printers (Gutenberg and his successors) were based in the south, this southern dialectal form became the established technical term for printing in the seventeenth century.

The semantic split is clean: ~drucken~ means "to print" (text, books, newspapers), while ~drücken~ means "to press, push" (a button, a hand). Both descend from the same Proto-Germanic root, but the printing revolution cemented two distinct verbs. The derived noun ~Druck~ can mean both "print" and "pressure," preserving the original unity. Polish ~drukować~ ("to print") was borrowed from German ~drucken~.
en.drängen:
From a merger of two Middle High German verbs: (1) MHG ~drengen~, from OHG ~drengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrangwijaną~; and (2) the now-obsolete ~drangen~, from MHG ~drangen~, from OHG ~drangōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangōn~. Both derive ultimately from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press, push") and, more distantly, with English ~throng~ (a pressing crowd).

The fact that two separate verbs merged into a single modern form is an unusual etymological event. The causative *~þrangwijaną~ ("to cause to press") and the denominative *~þrangōn~ ("to act like a press/crowd") converged because their meanings overlapped so thoroughly. The related strong verb ~dringen~ ("to penetrate, press through") preserves the intransitive sense, while ~drängen~ took over the transitive and causative meanings ("to push, urge, press someone"). The noun ~Drang~ ("urge, drive, pressure"), as in ~Sturm und Drang~ ("Storm and Stress"), the famous 18th-century literary movement, derives from the same root. The English word ~throng~ entered the language from Old Norse ~þrǫng~ ("crowd"), itself from the same Proto-Germanic family, making it a Scandinavian cousin of this purely West Germanic verb.
en.drücken: From Middle High German ~drücken~, from Old High German ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Low German ~drücken~, Old English ~þryċċan~ (surviving in dialectal English ~thrutch~). A striking consequence of the same root is the doublet within German itself: ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") descend from the same Old High German verb, with the printing sense arising from Gutenberg-era specialization of the pressing gesture. Welsh ~trychu~ ("to cut") and Lithuanian ~trū́kti~ ("to tear, burst") are cognates outside Germanic, illuminating the original sense of forceful rupture.
en.ehren:
From Middle High German ~ēren~, from Old High German ~ēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizāną~, from PIE *~h₂eys-~ ("to respect, to be in awe of"). Derived from the noun ~Ehre~ ("honor"), which descends from OHG ~ēra~ ("honor, fame, sense of honor"), from Proto-West Germanic *~aiʀu~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizō~. Cognate with Old Norse ~eir~ ("pardon, gentleness"), Old Saxon ~ēra~ ("honor, protection, pardon"), Old English ~ār~ ("honor, help, pardon"), and Dutch ~eer~ ("honor").

The verb ~ehren~ means "to honor, to respect, to pay tribute to." The connection to Latin ~aestimāre~ ("to value, to acknowledge"), whence English ~esteem~ and ~estimate~, has been proposed via the PIE root, suggesting that the Indo-European speakers linked the concept of honor with the act of valuation. The proverb ~Ehrlich währt am längsten~ ("Honesty lasts the longest") uses the derived adjective ~ehrlich~ ("honest," literally "honor-like"). The compound ~Ehrenamt~ ("honorary office, volunteer position") reflects the German cultural concept of unpaid civic duty performed for honor rather than payment — a cornerstone of German community life that has no single-word English equivalent. The expression ~jemandem die letzte Ehre erweisen~ ("to pay someone the last honor") refers to attending a funeral, connecting ~Ehre~ to rites of passage.
en.eignen:
From Middle High German ~eigenen~, from Old High German ~eiganen~, from Proto-Germanic *~aiginōną~, a denominative verb derived from *~aiganaz~ ("owned, one's own"), the past participle of *~aiganą~ ("to possess, own"), from PIE *~h₂eh₂óyḱe~, from *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession"). The verb ~eignen~ thus originally meant "to make one's own, to appropriate" — a sense still visible in the reflexive ~sich etwas aneignen~ ("to acquire, appropriate something for oneself"). The modern reflexive ~sich eignen~ ("to be suited, to be fit for") developed from the idea of being the proper or fitting owner of some quality or role.

The adjective ~eigen~ ("own, characteristic") shares the same PGmc root and is cognate with English ~own~ and Dutch ~eigen~. The PIE root *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession") also underlies Gothic ~aigan~ ("to have") and Old English ~āgan~ ("to own"), the latter giving English ~owe~ (its present tense) and ~ought~ (its past tense). Cognate with Swedish ~ägna~, English ~own~.
en.einigen:
From Middle High German ~einegen~, ~einigen~, from Old High German ~gieinīgen~. Compound of ~ein~ + ~-igen~:

- ~ein~: From MHG ~ein~, from OHG ~ein~ ("one"), from Proto-West Germanic *~ain~, from Proto-Germanic *~ainaz~, from PIE *~h₁óynos~ ("one, single"). Cognate with English ~one~, Dutch ~een~, Danish ~en~.
- ~-igen~: A denominal/deadjectival suffix forming verbs from adjectives or nouns.

The verb means "to unite, to agree" and reflexively ~sich einigen~ means "to come to an agreement." The derivation from ~ein~ ("one") is transparent: to ~einigen~ is to make ~einig~ ("united, in agreement"), which is to make parties into "one." The OHG form ~gieinīgen~ shows the ~gi-~ prefix (modern ~ge-~) that was common in Old High German for creating perfective or resultative verbs. The word is inseparable from German political history: ~die (Wieder)vereinigung~ ("the (Re)unification") of 1990 uses the same root, and the motto ~Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit~ ("Unity and Justice and Freedom") opens the German national anthem. The PIE root *~h₁óynos~ also gave Latin ~ūnus~ ("one"), whence English ~union~, ~unite~, and ~unanimous~.
en.enden:
From Middle High German ~enden~, from Old High German ~entōn~ ("to end, to complete, to die"), attested since the 8th century. A denominative verb derived from the noun ~Ende~:

~Ende~ traces to OHG ~enti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andī~, from Proto-Germanic *~andijaz~, from PIE *~h₂entíos~ ("front, forehead") — itself from *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front").

The semantic journey from "forehead" to "end" is one of the more surprising in Germanic etymology. The PIE root *~h₂ent-~ referred to the front of the head — the face turned outward, the foremost surface of a thing. In Proto-Germanic, this gave *~andijaz~, which came to mean the farthest extent of something — the outermost point, the frontier, the edge. As the word entered OHG it had already shifted from "front" to "extremity," and from "extremity" to "terminus": the end is the point at which a thing faces outward no further. German ~Ende~ and English ~end~ are exact cognates, both descending from this root. The same PIE root *~h₂ent-~ also appears in the German prefix ~ent-~ and in Latin ~ante~ ("before") — a reminder that "front" and "before" are closely allied concepts. The verb ~enden~ is a simple denominative: to end is to bring something to its ~Ende~. Its OHG antecedent ~entōn~ already carried the sense of dying — reaching the ultimate end — a usage preserved in literary German to this day.
en.ernten:
From Middle High German ~ernen~, from Old High German ~arnon~, from Proto-Germanic *~azanōną~. This verb is denominative, derived from the noun *~azaniz~ ("harvest"), from Proto-Indo-European *~seh1-~ ("to sow"). The modern form with ~-t-~ (first attested in MHG ~ernde~) stems from a merger with the related noun OHG ~arnōt~, from Proto-Germanic *~azanōdaz~.

Cognate with English ~earn~, which shares the same Proto-Germanic ancestor *~azanōną~ but diverged dramatically in meaning. The connection is that both words originally denoted reaping the fruits of labor: German preserved the agricultural sense ("to harvest"), while English generalized it to "to gain by labor." The PIE root *~seh1-~ ("to sow") also produced Latin ~semen~ ("seed") and English ~sow~ and ~seed~, making ~ernten~ a distant cousin of all of them.
en.fahren: From Middle High German ~varn~, ~varen~, from Old High German ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose broad original sense of "to go, travel" narrowed in Modern German to emphasize vehicular travel, while the older general sense of "going" survives in derivatives like ~Erfahrung~ ("experience," literally "a traveling through") and ~Gefahr~ ("danger," literally "a lying in wait on the journey"). The related causative ~führen~ ("to lead, to conduct") derives from the same root: the weak formation *~fōrijaną~ ("to cause to go"), built with the Proto-Germanic causative suffix *~-janą~, supplies the transitive counterpart to strong intransitive ~fahren~ — the same pattern as ~sitzen~/~setzen~, ~liegen~/~legen~, and ~fallen~/~fällen~. Cognate with Dutch ~varen~, English ~fare~, Danish ~fare~.
en.fallen: From Middle High German ~vallen~, from Old High German ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~. The ultimate PIE origin is uncertain; one proposed reconstruction connects it to a compound *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"), related to Ancient Greek ~apóllūmi~ ("to destroy, kill") and Lithuanian ~pùlti~ ("to fall, rush"). A class VII strong verb with a reduplicated past tense in Proto-Germanic. The semantic range of ~fallen~ has remained remarkably stable across two millennia — the word for a leaf falling in Old High German is the same word used today for falling in love (~sich verlieben~) or for a soldier falling in battle (~fallen im Krieg~). The related weak causative ~fällen~ ("to fell, to cause to fall") derives from the same root via the Proto-Germanic suffix *~-janą~ (*~fallijaną~); the umlaut a → ä is the trace of that formation — the same pattern as ~sitzen~/~setzen~ and ~liegen~/~legen~. Cognate with Low German ~fallen~, Dutch ~vallen~, English ~fall~, Danish ~falde~, Icelandic ~falla~, Swedish ~falla~.
en.fangen: ~fangen~ comes from Middle High German ~vāhen~, from Old High German ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, attach, fasten"). The original strong verb had the vowel pattern ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was borrowed from the past forms under the influence of Middle Low German ~vangen~, spreading through Central German dialects in the early modern period. The same analogical leveling shaped ~hängen~, though ~hängen~ completed the shift more quickly because it already had two variant verbs reinforcing each other. Cognate with English ~fang~ (originally "that which seizes"), Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~, and — more distantly — Albanian ~peng~ ("to hinder, hold captive"). The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ also produced Latin ~pangere~ ("to fix, fasten") and ~pax~ ("peace, compact"), making ~fangen~ a distant relative of English ~peace~.
en.fassen:
From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). Cognate with English ~fetch~.

The connection between ~fassen~ and English ~fetch~ is one of the more startling cognate pairs in the Germanic family: both descend from the same PIE root, yet they diverged dramatically — German keeping the sense of grasping and holding, English developing the sense of going to retrieve. The Proto-Germanic verb *~fatōną~ was a weak class 2 verb meaning "to hold, seize," and its descendants in German spread across an exceptionally rich idiomatic range: ~sich fassen~ ("to compose oneself, pull oneself together"), ~Fassung~ ("composure; version of a text"), ~unfassbar~ ("incomprehensible, literally ungraspable"), ~fassungslos~ ("speechless, stunned"), and the compound ~umfassen~ ("to encompass"). The cognitive metaphor of understanding as physical grasping runs deep: in German one ~fasst~ an idea, in English one ~grasps~ it, and in Latin one ~comprehendit~ it — all three verbs from different roots sharing the same bodily image. The noun ~Fass~ ("barrel, cask") shares the same root — a container that holds things. Note that ~fassen~ is not related to the English verb "to fast" (dietary abstinence), which derives from Proto-Germanic *~fastōną~ ("to hold firm, abstain") — a different root that produced a false-friend surface resemblance.
en.fechten: From MHG ~vëhten~ ("to fight"), from OHG ~fëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fehtaną~, perhaps from PIE *~peḱ-~ ("to pluck, comb"), though that last step is not secure. A class III strong verb (~fechten~, ~focht~, ~gefochten~); the ~o~ of the Präteritum was generalized from the old plural stem (OHG ~fuhtum~). Cognate with English ~fight~, Dutch ~vechten~, Low German ~fechten~, Danish ~fægte~. German narrowed the word to fencing while English kept the broad sense; the older breadth survives in the noun ~Gefecht~ ("engagement, combat").
en.fehlen: From Middle High German ~vælen~, ~velen~, ~valen~, borrowed from Old French ~faillir~ ("to fail, be lacking"), from Latin ~fallō~ ("to deceive, cause to stumble"), from PIE *~(s)gʷʰh₂el-~ ("to stumble"), with a semantic development from "to stumble" through "to deceive." This makes ~fehlen~ one of the relatively few common German verbs that entered the language via Old French rather than through Germanic inheritance — a legacy of medieval courtly and trade contact. The semantic shift from "to deceive" through "to fall short" to "to be missing, to be lacking" follows the trajectory of French ~faillir~: what fails is what is not there when needed. The same Latin root gives English ~fail~, ~false~, and ~fallible~. Cognate with English ~fail~, French ~faillir~, Italian ~fallire~.
en.feiern:
From Middle High German ~vīren~, from Old High German ~fīrōn~, a denominative verb derived from Old High German ~fīra~ (whence modern ~Feier~), itself borrowed from Latin ~fēriae~ ("religious holidays, festivals"). Cognate with Dutch ~vieren~.

Latin ~fēriae~ is from Proto-Italic *~fēsiās~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰéh₁s-yo-s~, derived from *~dʰéh₁s~ ("god, godhead, deity"). The same PIE root underlies Latin ~fēstus~ ("festive") — whence English ~feast~ and ~festival~ — and Ancient Greek ~theîos~ ("divine"). ~Feiern~ is thus one of the rare German verbs whose etymology leads directly into Latin and ultimately into the divine: a holiday (~Feiertag~) was originally a day set aside for the gods. The route from Latin into German passed through the early Christian church, which adopted the Roman calendar vocabulary for its own feast days. The modern sense of ~feiern~ — throwing a birthday party, celebrating New Year's — is secular, but the word retains its sacred pedigree. Cognate (distantly) with English ~feast~ and ~festival~ via the Latin root.
en.fertigen: From Middle High German ~vertigen~, ~vertegen~ ("to prepare, to make ready, to keep ready"), equivalent to ~fertig~ + ~-en~. The adjective ~fertig~ ("ready, finished") descends from MHG ~fertec~, from OHG ~fartīg~, from the noun ~fart~ ("journey"). The original meaning of ~fertig~ was "ready for a journey" — prepared, equipped — before broadening to "ready" and then "finished, done." The noun ~Fart~ comes from the same root as ~fahren~: Proto-Germanic *~farą~ ("journey"), from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with Dutch ~vaardig~ ("capable, swift"), Low German ~fardig~, Old English ~fierd~ ("expedition, military campaign"). ~Fertigen~ in modern German means "to manufacture, to produce" — especially in industrial and technical contexts (~Bauteile fertigen~, "to manufacture components"). The semantic arc from "journey-ready" to "manufactured" traces the cultural shift from a travel-based to a production-based economy: what was once preparedness for departure became readiness as a finished product.
en.filmen:
A denominative verb from ~Film~ + ~-en~. The noun ~Film~ was borrowed from English ~film~, which descends from Old English ~filmen~ ("membrane, thin skin"), from Proto-West Germanic *~filmin-~, from Proto-Germanic *~filmin-~ ("thin skin, membrane"), from Proto-Indo-European *~pel-mo-~ ("membrane"), from the root *~pel-~ ("to cover, skin").

In a charming etymological boomerang, the word traveled from Germanic to English, where it underwent a remarkable semantic shift -- from "membrane" to "thin coating" (1577) to "photographic coating" (1845) to "motion picture" (1895) -- before being borrowed back into German in the early twentieth century. Old English ~filmen~ meant "foreskin" or "caul," and no Anglo-Saxon could have imagined that this humble anatomical term would one day name an art form.
en.finanzieren: From ~Finanz~ + ~-ieren~. ~Finanz~ derives from French ~finance(s)~, from Middle French ~finer~ ("to pay a ransom, to settle a debt"), from ~fin~ ("end"), from Latin ~fīnis~ ("end, boundary, limit"). The semantic chain is elegant: a debt is "ended" by payment, so ~finance~ originally meant "an ending" — specifically, the ending of an obligation through payment. The sense shifted from "ransom payment" (mid-fifteenth century) to "taxation" (late fifteenth century) to "management of money" (eighteenth century). German naturalized the verb with the standard ~-ieren~ suffix, making ~finanzieren~ ("to finance, to fund") feel thoroughly German despite its Romance pedigree. The Latin root ~fīnis~ also gives German ~Finale~, ~Definition~, and ~Infinitiv~ — the last being a grammatical term meaning "the form without an ending," a fitting irony for a verb-conjugation app. Cognate with English ~finance~, French ~financer~, Italian ~finanziare~.
en.finden: From Middle High German ~vinden~, from Old High German ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The semantic development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels similar shifts in Slavic languages. Cognate with Bavarian ~findn~, Low German ~finden~, Dutch ~vinden~, English ~find~, Danish ~finde~.
en.flechten: From MHG ~vlëhten~, from OHG ~flëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~flehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~flehtaną~, from PIE *~pleḱ-~ ("to plait, weave"). A class III strong verb (~flechten~, ~flocht~, ~geflochten~), its Präteritum ~o~ generalized from the old plural stem. Cognate with Dutch ~vlechten~, Old Norse ~flétta~, Swedish ~fläta~, and probably English ~flax~ (the plant one plaits). The same PIE root reached English by the Latin road as well, through ~plectere~ and ~plicāre~: ~plait~, ~complex~, and ~ply~ are all cousins of ~Flechte~.
en.fliegen: ~fliegen~ comes from Middle High German ~vliegen~, from Old High German ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from Proto-Indo-European *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"). The PIE root *~plewk-~ is an extended form of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim"), which also produced ~fließen~ ("to flow"), Latin ~pluere~ ("to rain"), and Greek ~plein~ ("to sail"). Motion through a fluid medium — whether water or air — was once a single conceptual domain. The High German consonant shift turned Proto-Germanic *fl- into German fl- unchanged (labial fricatives were unaffected), but the vowel shift from Proto-Germanic *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of German Class II strong verbs. Cognate with Dutch ~vliegen~, English ~fly~, Danish ~flyve~, and Low German ~flegen~. Compare also Bavarian ~fliagn~, which preserves an older vowel.
en.fliehen:
From Middle High German ~vliehen~, from Old High German ~fliohan~ ("to flee"), from Proto-West Germanic *~fleuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuhaną~ ("to flee"), probably from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to fly, flee"), an enlargement of *~plew-~ ("to flow, run"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with English ~flee~ (from OE ~flēon~), Dutch ~vlieden~, and Gothic ~þliuhan~ (with secondary ~þ-~).

The PIE root *~plewk-~ is also the source of ~fliegen~ ("to fly") and ~Flucht~ ("flight, escape"), making ~fliehen~ and ~fliegen~ etymological siblings -- the original root encompassed rapid motion through any medium. The English cognates ~flee~ and ~fly~ mirror this German pair perfectly. Gothic ~þliuhan~ is puzzling: it shows an unexpected ~þ-~ (th-sound) where all other Germanic languages have ~f-~. Linguists debate whether the Gothic form preserves an archaic consonant or reflects a secondary change unique to Gothic. The noun ~Flüchtling~ ("refugee"), derived from ~Flucht~, entered international discourse during the European migration crisis of 2015 -- a word with five-thousand-year-old roots describing an experience as old as humanity itself.
en.fließen: From Middle High German ~vlieȥen~, from Old High German ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, to stream, to flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, to run, to swim"). A class II strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~. The PIE root *~plewd-~ produced an extensive water-vocabulary across Indo-European: Latin ~pluvia~ ("rain"), whence English ~pluvial~; Latvian ~plūdi~ ("flood"); Lithuanian ~pláuti~ ("to wash"); and Greek ~pleō~ ("I sail"). Within Germanic, the root gave English ~fleet~ (originally "a place where water flows," then the ships gathered there), ~float~, ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~ ("to flow," archaic/literary), Swedish ~flyta~ ("to float"), and Icelandic ~fljóta~. The zero-grade form *~flut-~ produced German ~Flut~ ("flood, high tide"), English ~flood~, and Dutch ~vloed~. The derived noun ~Fluss~ ("river") is literally "a flowing" — Germanic languages conceptualize rivers as the action of flowing made permanent, whereas Latin ~flūmen~ (from ~fluere~, "to flow," a different PIE root) took the same metaphorical path independently. The compound ~Einfluss~ ("influence") calques Latin ~influentia~ — a flowing-in of one thing upon another.
en.folgen: From Middle High German ~volgen~, from Old High German ~folgēn~ (attested from the 8th century, meaning "to follow, serve faithfully, pursue"), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~. The ultimate pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. The Old High German forms reveal an early semantic range that blended physical following, loyal service, and pursuit — reflecting the social structures of early Germanic society in which following a lord was the fundamental act of the ~comitatus~ (the warrior band). German ~folgen~ and English ~follow~ are doublets: both descend from the same Proto-Germanic root, but ~follow~ entered Middle English via Old Norse ~fylgja~ through Old English ~folgian~. Cognate with Dutch ~volgen~, English ~follow~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
en.fordern:
From Middle High German ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from Old High German ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"). The semantic development from "to push forward" to "to demand, claim" reflects the notion of asserting or advancing a claim. The PIE root *~per-~ is shared with the separable prefix ~vor-~ and with English ~forth~, ~forward~, and ~further~ — all sharing the spatial sense of moving ahead.

German learners must take care to distinguish ~fordern~ ("to demand") from the near-homophone ~fördern~ ("to promote, advance, support"). Despite their near-identical sound, they descend from the same Proto-Germanic root and once overlapped in meaning; the umlaut in ~fördern~ (from MHG ~vürdern~, OHG ~furdiren~, from PWGmc *~furþrijan~) marks its more specifically "forward-moving" sense, while ~fordern~ settled on the sense of making a forward claim or assertion. Cognate with English ~further~ (via the same PIE root), Dutch ~vorderen~.
en.formen: From Middle High German ~formen~, a denominative verb derived from the noun ~Form~, from Middle High German ~form~, borrowed from Latin ~forma~ ("shape, figure, appearance"). The ultimate origin of Latin ~forma~ is uncertain, but it may derive from Etruscan *~morma~, itself from Ancient Greek ~morphe~ ("shape, fashion, outward form"), with dissimilation of *~m-m~ to *~f-m~, as also seen in Latin ~formica~ ("ant") and ~formido~ ("scarecrow, ghost"). This Latin-to-Greek connection means that ~formen~ and English ~morph~ are distant cousins, both tracing back to the Greek concept of visible shape. The German ~-ieren~ suffix was not used here, unlike with many other Latin-derived verbs; instead German created a straightforward denominative from the noun, giving ~formen~ its clean, native-sounding conjugation. English ~form~ (both noun and verb) is a sibling borrowing from the same Latin source, arriving via Old French ~fourme~.
en.fragen: From Middle High German ~vrāgen~, from Old High German ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~/~frāhēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative derived from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"). The PIE root *~preḱ-~ is widespread and productive: it yields Latin ~precor~ ("I pray, beseech"), Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~ ("asks"), and Persian ~porsīdan~ ("to ask"). The -~h~- spellings in Old High German (~frahēn~) reflect a retention of the Proto-Germanic laryngeal trace; the ~-g-~ forms ultimately prevailed. Cognate with Saterland Frisian ~fräigje~, Dutch ~vragen~, Low German ~fragen~, English ~frain~ (archaic, "to ask, inquire"), Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
en.frieren: From MHG ~vriesen~ (beside ~vrieren~), from OHG ~friosan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~freusan~, from Proto-Germanic *~freusaną~, from PIE *~prews-~ ("to freeze, frost"). A class II strong verb (~frieren~, ~fror~, ~gefroren~). The ~r~ is not original: it arose by grammatischer Wechsel in the past forms and was then carried back into the infinitive, exactly as in ~verlieren~ — MHG still had ~vriesen~ beside ~vror~. Cognate with English ~freeze~ and ~frost~, Dutch ~vriezen~, Danish ~fryse~, and Latin ~pruīna~ ("hoarfrost").
en.fällen:
From Middle High German ~vellen~, from Old High German ~fellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallijaną~ ("to make fall"), a causative of *~fallaną~ ("to fall"), possibly from PIE *~h₃elh₁-~ ("to fall, to perish"), with a prefix *~h₂epo~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~fell~ (as in "to fell a tree"), Dutch ~vellen~.

The causative relationship between ~fallen~ ("to fall") and ~fällen~ ("to cause to fall, to fell") is a textbook example of the Proto-Germanic ~jan~-causative, exactly parallel to ~sitzen~/~setzen~ ("sit"/"set") and ~liegen~/~legen~ ("lie"/"lay"). The umlaut in ~fällen~ (a to ä) is the footprint of this ancient causative suffix, which contained a front vowel that pulled the root vowel forward. In modern German, ~fällen~ means both "to fell" (a tree) and "to render, to pass" (a judgment: ~ein Urteil fällen~). The judicial sense developed from the image of a decisive, downward stroke -- just as a tree is brought down with finality, so too is a verdict delivered. The PIE root *~h₃elh₁-~ may connect to Greek ~apollȳmi~ ("to destroy, to kill") and Latin ~aboleō~ ("to destroy"), though this etymology remains debated among specialists.
en.fördern: From Middle High German ~vürdern~, from Old High German ~furdiren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~furþrijan~ ("to move forward, to bring to the front"). A denominative of the archaic comparative adverb ~fürder~ ("further, forward"), itself from Proto-West Germanic *~forþar~, from PIE *~per-~ ("before, in front, first") with a comparative suffix. The modern spelling with ~ö~ — rather than the expected ~ü~ — arose through conflation with the related word ~vorder~ (whence modern ~fordern~, "to demand"), probably reinforced by Middle Low German ~vȫrder~ / ~vȫrderen~. The near-homophone pair ~fördern~ ("to promote, support") and ~fordern~ ("to demand") is a persistent pitfall even for native speakers and a nearly untranslatable distinction for learners. Cognate with English ~further~ (both as adverb and as verb "to further a cause"), Dutch ~vorderen~.
en.fügen: From Middle High German ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from Old High German ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, to attach, to fasten"). ~Fügen~ means "to join, to fit together" and, reflexively, "to submit, to comply" (~sich fügen~) — the person who ~sich fügt~ joins themselves to the arrangement of fate or authority. The noun ~Fügung~ means "decree of fate, providence" — events that have been joined together by a higher hand. ~Sich in sein Schicksal fügen~ ("to accept one's fate") is one of the great stoic phrases of the German language. The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ connects ~fügen~ to a surprisingly wide family: Latin ~pāx~ ("peace" — literally a state of being joined, fastened together) yields English ~peace~, ~pact~, and ~pacify~; Latin ~pangō~ ("to fasten, to fix") gives ~compact~ and ~page~ (a sheet fastened in a book). The archaic English verb ~fay~ ("to fit closely, to join") is a direct Germanic cognate of ~fügen~, from Old English ~fēgan~, though it survives today only in specialized carpentry usage. Dutch ~voegen~ ("to join, to add") is the living cognate. The distance from PIE "to fasten" to German "to accept one's fate" traces a philosophical journey: what is fastened together by destiny cannot be unfastened by human will.
en.fühlen: From northern Middle High German ~vüelen~ (generally spelled ~vulen~), from Old High German ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"). The ultimate etymology is uncertain; the root is presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope, feel; to be astonished"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong verb *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Possible cognates include Latin ~palpō~ ("to stroke, soothe") and Ancient Greek ~psēlaphāō~ ("to feel, grope"). Upper German dialects of Middle High German used ~enphinden~ instead; Modern German ~empfinden~ ("to sense, perceive") has been chiefly confined to higher register as a result, while ~fühlen~ dominates everyday speech. Cognate with Dutch ~voelen~, English ~feel~, Danish ~føle~.
en.führen: From Middle High German ~vüeren~, from Old High German ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). The causative formation — "to make go," hence "to lead" — follows a productive Germanic pattern in which a long-vowel derivative of a strong verb creates a new weak verb with transitive meaning. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
en.füllen: ~Füllen~ ("to fill") descends from Middle High German ~vüllen~, Old High German ~fullen~, and Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"). This is the causative formation of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from Proto-Indo-European *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). Cognates include Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~, and English ~fill~ — all from the identical Proto-Germanic causative. English ~fill~ and German ~füllen~ are thus perfect cognates: each is the causative of its native word for "full" (*~full~ / ~voll~), with the characteristic Proto-Germanic causative suffix *~-ijaną~. Latin ~plenus~ ("full") descends from the same PIE root, giving English ~plenty~, ~complete~, and ~replenish~. The simple parallel — "to full" meaning "to make full" — survived intact in both West Germanic branches.
en.füttern:
From Middle High German ~vuotern~, from Old High German ~fuotiren~, derived from the noun ~fuotar~ ("fodder"), from Proto-Germanic *~fōdrą~ ("fodder"), from Proto-Indo-European *~peh2-~ ("to guard, graze, feed"). Equivalent to ~Futter~ + ~-n~. Cognate with English dialectal ~to fodder~, Dutch ~voeren~ ("to feed").

There is a second, homonymous ~füttern~ meaning "to line (a garment)," also from MHG ~vuotern~, but derived from a different (though probably distantly related) noun OHG ~fuotar~ ("sheath, wrapping, lining"). The PIE root *~peh2-~ ("to feed, to guard") is remarkably productive: it also gave rise to English ~food~, ~feed~, ~foster~, ~pasture~, and Latin ~pābulum~ ("food, fodder") and ~pāstor~ ("shepherd") -- the shepherd being, at root, the feeder.
en.geben: From Middle High German ~gëben~, from Old High German ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with Dutch ~geven~, English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
en.gehen: From Middle High German ~gan~, ~gen~, from Old High German ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The conjugation ~gen~ instead of ~gan~ is of Bavarian origin. The ~-h-~ was introduced into the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~, in which it had become mute but was retained in spelling. Cognate with Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gaan~, ~gahn~, English ~go~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
en.gelten: From Middle High German ~gelten~, from Old High German ~geltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~geldaną~, possibly from PIE *~gʰeldʰ-~. The semantic range has narrowed over time: in Old High German, ~geltan~ meant "to pay, repay, be worth," while Modern German ~gelten~ centers on "to be valid, to count, to apply." Cognate with Dutch ~gelden~, English ~yield~ (from the same root, with a semantic shift from "paying" to "giving way"), Icelandic ~gjalda~.
en.gießen:
From Middle High German ~giezen~, from Old High German ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour").

Cognate with Dutch ~gieten~, Old Saxon ~giotan~, Old English ~geotan~, Old Norse ~gjota~ (whence Danish ~gyde~, Swedish ~gjuta~), Gothic ~giutan~. Further Indo-European cognates include Latin ~fundō~ ("to pour, to smelt"), Greek ~cheo~ ("to pour"), and Sanskrit ~juhoti~ ("he sacrifices" -- by pouring libations). English ~gush~ is a related form.

The sense of "pouring" metals and glass is attested since Old High German times through the participle ~gigozzan~ ("poured, cast"). This makes ~gießen~ one of the oldest technical terms still in daily use: a ~Gießkanne~ ("watering can") and a ~Gießerei~ ("foundry") both preserve the ancient act of controlled pouring. The connection to Latin ~fundō~ (whence English ~found~, as in founding metals, ~foundry~, and ~fusion~) shows that pouring and casting were among the earliest specialized activities to receive their own vocabulary across the Indo-European world.
en.gleichen:
From MHG ~gelīchen~, from OHG ~gilīhhon~, ~gilihhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkōną~ ("to make alike, to resemble"), derived from *~galīkaz~ ("alike, similar"), a compound of *~ga-~ (collective prefix) + *~līkam~ ("body, form"), from PIE *~leyg-~ ("image, likeness, similarity"). Cognate with Dutch ~gelijken~, English ~like~ (both the adjective and the verb), Old English ~gelīcian~ ("to please") and ~gelīc~ ("alike"), Old Norse ~glíkr~, Danish ~ligne~.

~Gleichen~ means "to resemble, to be equal to" and is a strong verb (glich, geglichen), one of the few strong verbs derived from a denominal/deadjectival base. The adjective ~gleich~ ("equal, same, alike") lost its prefix ~ge-~ through phonetic erosion in Early New High German, but the verb preserved it as the initial ~gl-~. The underlying metaphor is illuminating: PIE *~leyg-~ meant "body, form" — to be alike was originally to share the same bodily form. This root produced English ~like~, ~alike~, ~likeness~, ~lich~ (a corpse — literally "a body"), the suffix ~-ly~ (originally "having the body/form of"), and ~ilk~ ("same kind"). The word ~like~ in English descends from the same Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, meaning that ~gleichen~ and ~like~ are doublets — siblings that traveled different phonetic paths from the same ancestor.
en.gleiten: From MHG ~glīten~, from OHG ~glītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~glīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~glīdaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰleydʰ-~ ("to glide, slide"). A class I strong verb (~gleiten~, ~glitt~, ~geglitten~), though a weak ~gleitete~ turns up in technical prose. Cognate with English ~glide~, Dutch ~glijden~, Low German ~glieden~, Swedish ~glida~.
en.glimmen: From MHG ~glimmen~ ("to glow, gleam"), from Proto-Germanic *~glimmaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰley-~ ("to shine, shimmer"). Modern German inflects it both ways: the strong ~glomm~, ~geglommen~ has held on in written and elevated register, while weak ~glimmte~, ~geglimmt~ has dominated ordinary usage since the eighteenth century. Cognate with English ~gleam~, ~glimmer~, and ~glimpse~, Dutch ~glimmen~, Norwegian ~glime~. Its root belongs to the unusually large and unusually consistent Germanic ~gl-~ family of light words — ~Glanz~, ~glühen~, ~Glas~, English ~glow~ and ~glitter~ — all extensions of PIE *~ǵʰel-~.
en.glänzen:
From Middle High German ~glenzen~, from Old High German ~glanzen~, from Proto-Germanic *~glantaz~ ("shining, bright"), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰlond-o-~, from the root *~gʰlend-~ ("to shine, to gleam").

This verb belongs to a rich cluster of Germanic "gl-" words denoting light and vision: ~gleißen~ ("to glitter"), ~glimmen~ ("to glow"), ~glitzern~ ("to sparkle"), ~Glut~ ("embers"), and ~Glas~ ("glass," originally meaning "amber" or "something shiny"). English preserves the same pattern in ~gleam~, ~glitter~, ~glow~, ~gloss~, ~glint~, and ~glisten~. This "gl-" phonestheme -- where an initial consonant cluster carries consistent semantic associations without being a true morpheme -- is one of the most striking sound-meaning patterns in the Germanic languages.
en.graben: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~, and English ~grave~ as a verb ("to dig, to engrave"), which has otherwise died out and survives only in ~engrave~ and the phrase ~graven image~. Where English kept just the noun, German kept the whole family alive — ~Grab~, ~Graben~, ~Grube~ — and Polish ~grzebać~ ("to bury") shows the root reaching well beyond Germanic.
en.greifen:
From Middle High German ~grîfen~, from Old High German ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, English ~gripe~, and Old Norse ~gripa~.

The PIE root *~gʰreyb-~ is attested in Baltic cognates as well: Lithuanian ~griẽbti~ ("to seize") and ~graibýti~ share the same ancestry, as does Latvian ~gribêt~ ("to wish, desire") — a striking semantic divergence in which the Baltic branch preserved a sense of striving or wanting from what was originally a physical act of grasping. German has developed ~greifen~ into a rich family of compounds: ~begreifen~ ("to comprehend," literally "to grasp around"), ~eingreifen~ ("to intervene," literally "to grasp in"), ~angreifen~ ("to attack, to corrode"), and ~ergreifen~ ("to seize, to move emotionally"). The idea that understanding is a form of grasping — ~begreifen~ — is one of the most striking conceptual metaphors in the language, and it is ancient. The ablaut series ~greift~/~griff~/~gegriffen~ follows the class I pattern, the same as ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~.
en.gründen:
Inherited from Middle High German ~gründen~, from Old High German ~grunten~ ("to fathom, to investigate"). A denominative verb formed from ~Grund~ ("ground, bottom, foundation") with derivational umlaut (u → ü):

~Grund~ traces to OHG ~grunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grundu~, from Proto-Germanic *~grunduz~, from PIE *~gʰr̥mtu-~. Cognate with West Frisian ~grûn~, Dutch ~grond~, and English ~ground~.

The OHG verb ~grunten~ meant "to fathom" — to sound the depth of water, to investigate the bottom of a matter. This sense still echoes in ~ergründen~ ("to fathom, to get to the bottom of something"). ~gründen~, by contrast, shifted from probing the ground to creating it: "to found, to establish" — to put something on a secure foundation. The same metaphor appears in English ~ground~ (as in "to ground one's argument"). The umlaut — ~Grund~ → ~gründen~ — is a hallmark of denominative weak verbs in German: it signals that the verb was derived from the noun rather than inherited directly. The noun ~Grund~ itself remains semantically rich: it serves simultaneously as "ground" (the earth underfoot), "bottom" (the floor of a lake), "reason" (the ground of an argument), and "foundation" (the basis of a building) — all the more remarkable because these senses converge in a single word that goes back to a PIE root simply meaning "earth, soil." Cognate with Dutch ~gronden~.
en.gucken:
From Middle High German ~gücken~, ~guggen~ ("to look inquisitively, to peek, to peer"), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a specialized use of MHG ~gücken~, ~gucken~ ("to cuckoo, to call or cry like a cuckoo"), from Old High German ~guckōn~, ~gukkōn~ ("to cuckoo") — the semantic link being the cuckoo's habit of poking its head out from cover, or the notion of peeping out curiously. The common pronunciation with initial ~k-~ (also spelled ~kucken~) is often attributed to influence from Low German ~kieken~ (from Middle Low German ~kīken~), though this pronunciation extends surprisingly far southward (compare Luxembourgish ~kucken~ and Dutch ~kijken~).

~Gucken~ is the everyday, colloquial word for "to look" in northern and central Germany, while southern German and Austrian varieties prefer ~schauen~. It rarely appears in formal writing, where ~sehen~, ~blicken~, or ~schauen~ take its place. Despite its informal register, ~gucken~ is enormously productive: ~angucken~ ("to look at"), ~zugucken~ ("to watch"), ~weggucken~ ("to look away"), ~durchgucken~ ("to look through"), ~Guckloch~ ("peephole"). The compound ~Kuckuck~ ("cuckoo") — if the etymological connection holds — would make ~gucken~ one of the few verbs potentially derived from a bird's call. The spelling debate between ~gucken~ (standard) and ~kucken~ (reflecting actual pronunciation) has generated more heat among German orthography enthusiasts than one might expect for a monosyllabic verb.
en.gären: From MHG ~jesen~, from OHG ~jesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~jesaną~, from PIE *~yes-~ ("to boil, foam, ferment"). Two changes produced the modern shape: the initial ~j-~ hardened to ~g-~ before front vowels from Middle High German on, and the ~r~ was carried in from the past forms ~gor~, ~gegoren~ (as in ~verlieren~), reinforced by association with the unrelated adjective ~gar~ ("done, fully cooked"). Historically a class V strong verb; the modern ~gor~/~gegoren~ vocalism is analogical, and today the strong forms are usual for literal fermenting while the weak ~gärte~, ~gegärt~ is preferred figuratively (~es gärte im Volk~). Cognate with English ~yeast~, German ~Gischt~ ("spray, foam"), and Ancient Greek ~ζέω~ (zéō, "to boil").
en.gönnen:
From MHG ~gunnen~, from OHG ~giunnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gaunnan~ ("to grant"), from the prefix *~ga-~ + *~unnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~unnaną~ ("to grant"), from PIE *~h₃neh₂-~ ("to enjoy"). Cognate with Dutch ~gunnen~, Yiddish ~ginen~. The PIE root also appears in Greek ~oninēmi~ ("to be of use, to help") and ~aponēto~ ("to have joy of something").

~Gönnen~ is one of those German words that English simply cannot translate with a single term. It means "to not begrudge someone something" — to be genuinely happy that another person has or enjoys something. ~Ich gönne dir den Erfolg~ means "I'm happy for your success" with no trace of envy. The negation ~missgönnen~ ("to begrudge, to envy") and the noun ~Missgunst~ ("envy, resentment") expose the default expectation: ~Gunst~ ("favor, goodwill") is the positive baseline. The reflexive ~sich etwas gönnen~ means "to treat oneself, to allow oneself a pleasure" — again, granting oneself permission to enjoy. The PIE root *~h₃neh₂-~ ("to enjoy") has been remarkably faithful to its original meaning across five millennia, even as the social dimension — the emphasis on non-envious generosity — is a distinctly Germanic innovation.
en.haben:
From Middle High German ~haben~, from Old High German ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Cognate with Dutch ~hebben~, English ~have~, Danish ~have~, Old Norse ~hafa~, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (~haban~).

~Haben~ and Latin ~habēō~ ("to have") are one of the most celebrated false-cognate pairs in Indo-European linguistics. Despite near-identical spelling, identical meaning, and centuries of scholarly confusion, the two words descend from entirely different PIE roots: ~haben~ from *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize") and ~habēō~ from *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ ("to grab, take"). The resemblance is pure coincidence — the kind of accident that makes historical linguistics treacherous. ~Haben~'s actual Latin cousin is ~capiō~ ("I take, I seize"), the ancestor of English ~captive~, ~capture~, ~capable~, ~captain~, and ~accept~ (from ~ad-~ + ~capiō~). German ~akzeptieren~ thus descends from the same PIE root as ~haben~, via Latin rather than Germanic inheritance. The same root also gives German ~heben~ ("to lift") — to have and to heave are, at bottom, the same word: to grasp something is both to possess it and to lift it.

Perhaps the deepest irony is that Germanic and Romance languages independently chose their respective "have" verbs — etymologically unrelated — to build compound past tenses: German ~ich habe gesungen~ and French ~j'ai chanté~ are structurally identical constructions ("I have sung"), yet ~haben~ and ~avoir~ (from ~habēō~) share no common ancestor. This parallel development is a hallmark of the Western European ~Sprachbund~ — a linguistic area in which neighboring but unrelated languages converge on shared grammatical structures through centuries of contact. The ~Sprachbund~ also produced the definite article, the relative clause with a relative pronoun, and the distinction between ~sein~ and ~haben~ as perfect auxiliaries (compare French ~je suis allé~ / ~j'ai mangé~ with German ~ich bin gegangen~ / ~ich habe gegessen~) — all features that feel natural to European speakers but are typologically unusual worldwide. That two unrelated "have" verbs independently became the scaffolding for compound tenses across the Roman ~limes~ is a reminder that grammar can be borrowed just as readily as vocabulary.
en.haften:
From ~Haft~ + ~-en~. ~Haft~ descends from MHG ~haft~, ~hafte~ ("captivity"), from OHG ~haft~, ~hafta~, immediately cognate with Middle Dutch ~hachte~, Middle Low German ~hafte~, Old English ~hæft~ ("captive"), and further with Latin ~captus~ ("seized") and Old Irish ~cacht~ ("captive"). The Latin and Germanic forms both derive from PIE *~kh₂p-tó-~ (from *~keh₂p-~ "to seize, grasp"), making ~haften~ and English ~captive~ cognates from the same root.

~Haften~ means "to stick, adhere, cling" and "to be liable, to be responsible" -- two senses united by the "captivity" root. The "adhesion" sense developed from the idea of being held fast, clinging to a surface. The legal meaning is especially productive: ~haftbar~ ("liable"), ~Haftpflicht~ ("liability"), ~Haftpflichtversicherung~ ("liability insurance"), and ~Haft~ itself now primarily means "custody, imprisonment." That Latin ~captus~ and Germanic ~haft~ are cognates is beautifully confirmed by the same semantic range: both moved from "seized" to "held" to "bound."
en.halten: From Middle High German ~halten~, from Old High German ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with Bavarian ~hoidn~, Low German ~holden~, Dutch ~houden~, English ~hold~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
en.handeln: From Middle High German ~handeln~, from Old High German ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb derived from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~. The underlying noun ~Hand~ traces from MHG ~hant~, from OHG ~hant~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handu~, from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~. The semantic development from "to handle (with the hand)" to "to act, deal, trade" reflects a concrete-to-abstract broadening typical of denominative verbs. Cognate with Dutch ~handelen~, English ~handle~, Danish ~handle~, Swedish ~handla~.
en.hassen:
From Middle High German ~hazzen~, from Old High German ~hazzon~, from Proto-Germanic *~hatāną~, a stative-fientive verb derived from *~hataz~ ("hate, hostility"), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh2d-~ ("grief, hatred").

Cognate with English ~hate~, Dutch ~haten~, Old Norse ~hata~, Gothic ~hatan~. The PIE root *~keh2d-~ also produced Greek ~kēdos~ ("care, grief, mourning") and Welsh ~cas~ ("hatred"). The Proto-Germanic noun *~hataz~ survives in Old English ~hete~ and is the source of English ~hate~. Interestingly, the Greek descendant ~kēdos~ developed in the opposite emotional direction, coming to mean "care, concern" and eventually "funeral rites" -- suggesting that the PIE root may have originally denoted intense emotional engagement rather than a specific negative emotion.
en.hauen:
From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Cognate with English ~hew~.

~Hauen~ means "to hit, to strike, to chop, to hew" and is one of German's oldest action verbs. Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), it has partially weakened in colloquial speech, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~ as the past tense. In everyday German, ~hauen~ is the child's word for hitting: ~Er hat mich gehauen!~ ("He hit me!") is the universal playground complaint. But the verb also has a vigorous literary and technical life: ~in Stein hauen~ ("to carve in stone"), ~Holz hauen~ ("to chop wood"), ~hau ab!~ ("beat it!, get lost!"). The English cognate ~hew~ has retained the more dignified "chop, carve" meaning. The PIE root *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, forge") also connects to Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, to forge").
en.heben:
From Middle High German ~heben~, ~heven~, from Old High German ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb; the past tense ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ descend from the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~, Swedish ~häva~.

The curious shift from "to seize" (PIE) to "to lift" (Germanic) reflects the same conceptual move as in English ~heave~ — the act of taking hold of something is inseparable from lifting it. The same PIE root *~keh₂p-~ also produced Latin ~capiō~ ("I take, I seize"), giving English ~capture~, ~capable~, ~captain~, and — via the frequentative ~acceptāre~ — German ~akzeptieren~. So ~heben~ and ~akzeptieren~, despite looking nothing alike, are distant PIE cousins: both descend from the same ancient root meaning "to grasp." The derived noun ~Hebel~ ("lever") preserves the physical mechanics of the verb: a lever is the tool that lifts. Cognate with Dutch ~heffen~, English ~heave~.
en.hehlen: From MHG ~heln~, from OHG ~helan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helaną~, from PIE *~ḱel-~ ("to cover, conceal"). Originally a class IV strong verb (OHG ~helan~, ~hal~, ~gaholan~); modern German conjugates it weak (~hehlte~, ~gehehlt~). Cognate with Old English ~helan~ ("to conceal"), Latin ~cēlāre~ and ~occulere~, Ancient Greek ~kalýptein~ ("to cover"); the same root yields ~Helm~, ~Hülle~ and ~Hölle~, hell being named as the covering, sheltering place. The old strong participle survives as an adjective in ~verhohlen~ and ~unverhohlen~ ("undisguised") — a fossil of a conjugation the verb itself has abandoned.
en.heilen:
From Middle High German ~heilen~, from Old High German ~heilen~ (causative, "to make whole") and ~heilēn~ (inchoative, "to become whole"), from Proto-West Germanic *~hailijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hailijaną~ ("to heal, make whole, save"), derived from *~hailaz~ ("whole, healthy, uninjured"), from PIE *~kéh₂ilos~ ("healthy, whole"). Cognate with English ~heal~ (from OE ~hǣlan~), Dutch ~helen~, Old Norse ~heila~.

The adjective ~heil~ ("whole, sound") is the source of both ~heilen~ and English ~whole~ (from OE ~hāl~, with the same meaning). The ~w-~ in ~whole~ is a late English spelling addition; historically ~hale~ and ~whole~ are the same word. English ~hale~ ("robust, healthy") preserves the original form. The connection between wholeness and health runs deep: to ~heilen~ is to restore something to its ~heile~ ("whole") state. The word ~heilig~ ("holy") is also from ~heil~ -- to be holy is, etymologically, to be whole and inviolate.
en.heißen: From Middle High German ~heiȥen~, from Old High German ~heiȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haitan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haitaną~, tentatively from PIE *~ḱeyd-~ ("to call"). The original sense was "to command, order" (still preserved in the construction ~jemanden etwas heißen~), with the meaning "to be called, be named" developing from the passive use: "to be called (something)" became the dominant sense. Cognate with Bavarian ~haßn~, ~hoaßn~, Yiddish ~heysn~, Dutch ~heten~, Low German ~heten~, ~heiten~, Old Norse ~heita~, Gothic ~haitan~. The most direct English cognate is the archaic verb ~hight~ ("called, named"), from Old English ~hātan~, which survives in Spenser and other early-modern poets (~a goodly knight, hight George~). Like ~heißen~, it froze in the passive sense "to be called." Also cognate with English ~hest~, ~behest~, which preserve the original "command" meaning.
en.helfen: From Middle High German ~hëlfen~, from Old High German ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with Low German ~helpen~, Dutch ~helpen~, English ~help~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
en.herrschen:
From MHG ~hērschen~, ~hērsen~, from OHG ~hērrisōn~, ~hērisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hairisōn~ ("to be strong, to dominate"). The surface form was remodeled after ~Herr~ already during the MHG period.

~Herr~ itself descends from MHG ~hērre~, OHG ~hēriro~ / ~hērro~, originally the comparative of ~hēr~ ("grey-haired, noble, venerable"), from Proto-Germanic *~hairaz~ ("grey"). Cognates: Dutch ~heer~, Old English ~hār~, English ~hoar~ and ~hoary~, Old Norse ~hárr~. The same root also gives modern German ~hehr~ ("sublime, noble") — so ~Herr~, ~herrschen~, ~herrlich~, and ~Herrschaft~ all descend from an ancestral word meaning "grey-haired," the authority of an elder embedded in each.
en.hindern: From Middle High German ~hindern~, from Old High German ~hintaren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hindrōną~ ("to hinder"), derived from the adverb *~hinder~ ("back, behind"). The adverb itself likely comes from PIE *~ḱem-tér-~ ("down, back, through"), from *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near"), though an alternative theory derives it from *~ḱís~ ("this"). The semantic path from "behind" to "to obstruct" is intuitive: what is behind you blocks the way forward. Cognate with English ~hinder~, Dutch ~hinderen~. The related Latin ~contrā~ ("against") descends from the same PIE root, making ~hindern~ a distant cousin of English ~counter~ and ~contrary~.
en.hoffen:
From Middle High German ~hoffen~ (first attested 12th century), from northern Old High German *~hoffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hopōn~. The ultimate pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. The word's early attestation is exclusively in northern and central German dialects; it was absent from Upper German, where it only became established in later Middle High German, gradually displacing the now-obsolete ~gedingen~ ("to have hope, trust"). Some scholars have proposed that all continental Germanic forms derive from Old English ~hopian~, introduced to the continent by Anglo-Saxon missionaries — which would make ~hoffen~ a remarkably late addition to the German vocabulary, arriving through religious rather than inherited channels.

Whether missionary loan or parallel inheritance, the word displaced a native competitor (~gedingen~, related to ~Ding~, "thing, assembly") and established itself as the sole common word for hope in German. Its exact PIE ancestry remains debated, with no secure cognate outside Germanic. Cognate with Dutch ~hopen~, English ~hope~, Danish ~håbe~, Swedish ~hoppas~, Yiddish ~האָפֿן~ (~hofn~).
en.holen: From Middle High German ~holen~, ~holn~, from Old High German ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get, draw"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, cry, summon"). The semantic development would be from "to summon, call (someone to come)" → "to go and fetch, retrieve." The connection to PIE *~kelh₁-~ is uncertain but paralleled by similar "call → fetch" developments in other languages. Wiktionary directs readers to English ~haul~ for related forms. The cognate English word ~haul~ (from Old French ~haler~, of Germanic origin) shares the sense of pulling something toward oneself, pointing to an underlying idea of directed movement. Cognate with Low German ~halen~, Dutch ~halen~ ("to fetch, get"), English ~haul~ (via French).
en.hängen:
Modern German ~hängen~ is the result of the gradual merger of three historically distinct Old High German verbs, all related in meaning and ancestry:

1. OHG ~hāhan~ (strong, chiefly transitive), past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~ — the original strong verb meaning "to be suspended."
2. OHG ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive) — a related form also meaning "to hang."
3. OHG ~hengen~ (weak, transitive/causative), from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~ — a causative formation meaning "to hang something, to cause to hang."

Verbs 1 and 2 merged first, combining the present stem ~hang-~ from ~hangēn~ with the strong past forms (~hing~, ~gehangen~) of ~hāhan~. This merger is first attested in the north and spread southward through Middle Low German and into Central German during the 14th century. The causative verb 3 — ancestor of modern transitive ~hängen~ — was kept formally separate into the 20th century, at least by prescriptive grammarians, but colloquial usage steadily conflated all three. Today the distinction is upheld primarily in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ ("the coat was hanging") versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~ ("she hung the coat"). This mirrors the English ~lie~/~lay~ distinction, which likewise collapses in casual speech. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
en.hören: From Middle High German ~hœren~, from Old High German ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). The PIE root is a compound construction meaning literally "to have sharp ears" — a vivid image of acute hearing built into the very fabric of the word. Cognate with Dutch ~horen~, English ~hear~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
en.jagen:
From MHG ~jagen~ ("to hurry, drive, pursue, hunt"), from OHG ~jagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~jagōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~jakkōną~. The Proto-Germanic form derives from a ~nā~-iterative formation, likely rebuilt from PIE *~h₁eyǵʰ-~ ("to strive, chase"). Attested since the eighth century. Further pre-Germanic etymology is obscure.

~Jagen~ means "to hunt, to chase, to drive" and is one of the oldest action verbs in the Germanic lexicon, reflecting the centrality of hunting to early Germanic society. The noun ~Jagd~ ("hunt") derives from the same root and appears in countless compounds: ~Jagdhund~ ("hunting dog"), ~Jagdhorn~ ("hunting horn"), ~Jagdrevier~ ("hunting grounds"). The verb has developed rich figurative uses: ~jemanden aus dem Amt jagen~ ("to chase someone out of office"), ~einen Schauer über den Rücken jagen~ ("to send a shiver down someone's spine"). The compound ~Jäger~ ("hunter") is also famous as a military term -- ~Jäger~ units were light infantry in the Prussian and Austrian armies, originally recruited from professional hunters and gamekeepers.
en.kaufen: From Middle High German ~koufen~, from Old High German ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb derived from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"). *~kaupô~ is a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper, petty trader"), itself likely a common Mediterranean trade word. This Latin borrowing entered Germanic during the period of Roman-Germanic commercial contact along the Rhine and Danube frontiers. The word spread widely: Old English ~cēapian~ ("to trade, buy") yielded ~cheap~ — originally meaning "bargain, price, trade" (as in the London market district ~Cheapside~) — and the place-name element ~Chipping-~ appears in English market towns (Chipping Norton, Chipping Campden). The Danish capital ~København~ ("Copenhagen") literally means "merchants' harbor": *~kaupô~ + *~hafnō~ ("harbor"). Cognate with Dutch ~kopen~, English ~cheap~ and ~cheapen~, Danish ~købe~, Swedish ~köpa~, Icelandic ~kaupa~. Related to German ~Kauf~ ("purchase") and ~verkaufen~ ("to sell").
en.kehren: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1), "to turn," comes from Middle High German ~kēren~, from Old High German ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin — possibly connected to PIE *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"), though Kluge's etymological dictionary calls this "a difficult word to explain both etymologically and phonetically." ~Kehren~ (2), "to sweep," comes from Middle High German ~kern~, ~keren~, from Old High German ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Despite their identical modern forms, these are etymologically unrelated verbs that merged through phonological convergence. The "turn" sense survives in ~umkehren~ ("to turn around, to reverse"), ~Kehrtwendung~ ("about-face"), ~zurückkehren~ ("to return"), and the idiom ~den Rücken kehren~ ("to turn one's back"). The "sweep" sense lives in ~auskehren~ ("to sweep out"), ~Kehricht~ ("sweepings, rubbish"), and the compound ~Kehrwoche~ — the famously Swabian tradition where apartment residents take turns sweeping shared spaces on a rotating schedule. English ~car~ (via Latin ~carrus~) is not related, despite superficial similarity.
en.keifen: From MHG ~kīben~, from OHG *~kīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kīban~ ("to quarrel"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. MHG ~kīben~ was a class I strong verb, but modern ~keifen~ is conjugated weak (~keifte~, ~gekeift~). The ~-f-~ is an import from Low and West Central German; the original stop is still audible in the Upper German iteratives ~kibbeln~ and ~keppeln~. Cognate with Dutch ~kijven~, Middle Low German ~kīven~.
en.kennen: From Middle High German ~kennen~, from Old High German ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~ ("to know"), from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to know"), a causative form of *~kunnaną~ with the suffix *~-janą~. *~kunnaną~ derives from PIE *~ǵn̥néh₃ti~, from *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). The causative origin means ~kennen~ originally signified "to make known, to cause to know" before narrowing to "to know, be acquainted with." Cognate with Bavarian ~kennan~, Dutch ~kennen~, Low German ~kennen~, Scots and English ~ken~ ("to know"). ~Kennen~ is a member of the Rückumlaut cohort: the present shows umlaut (~ich kenne~), but the preterite does not (~kannte~, ~gekannt~). Other members: ~brennen~, ~nennen~, ~rennen~, ~senden~, ~wenden~, ~denken~, ~bringen~ — see ~brennen~ for the fuller explanation.
en.klagen: From Middle High German ~klagen~, from Old High German ~klagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klagōn~ ("to lament, complain"), a denominative verb from *~klagu~ ("lamentation, complaint"). The ultimate origin is uncertain; it is often compared to Proto-Indo-Iranian *~garjʰ-~ ("to complain"), but phonological difficulties make this connection questionable, and some scholars favor an onomatopoeic origin -- the word imitating the sound of wailing. German ~klagen~ preserves both the emotional sense ("to lament, mourn") and a legal one ("to sue, file a complaint"), whence the noun ~Klage~ means both "lament" and "lawsuit." English ~claim~ is unrelated, coming instead from Latin ~clāmāre~.
en.klappen: From Middle Low German ~klappen~, from Old Saxon *~klappōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klappōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klappōną~. The verb is onomatopoeic — it imitates the sharp percussive sound of a flat surface snapping shut. Cognate with Dutch ~klappen~ ("to clap, snap"), English ~clap~, and Old High German ~klapfō~ ("a clapping sound"). Also related to ~klaffen~ ("to gape, stand wide open"), which represents the same root shifted toward the open position rather than the shut one. The modern senses of ~klappen~ span the acoustic original ("to clatter, snap"), a physical result ("to fold shut"), and an abstract success meaning — "es klappt" ("it works out, it clicks") — where the satisfying snap of something fitting together became a metaphor for things going smoothly.
en.kleben:
From Middle High German ~kleben~, from Old High German ~klebēn~ ("to stick"), from Proto-West Germanic *~klibēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klibēną~, from PIE *~gleyb-~ ("to stick, adhere"). This is a durative formation from the strong verb root *~kleibēną~ ("to adhere, to climb"), with cognates in Old English ~cleofian~ ("to cleave to, adhere"), Old Norse ~klīfa~ ("to climb"), and Old High German ~-klīban~ ("to stick").

The PIE root *~gleyb-~ reveals a surprising family reunion: German ~kleben~ ("to stick"), English ~cleave~ (in the sense "to cling to"), and ~climb~ (from OE ~climban~, originally "to cling one's way upward") are all cousins. The relationship between sticking and climbing is intuitive -- to climb a cliff face, one must cling to it. Even more remarkably, English has two verbs spelled ~cleave~ with opposite meanings: "to cling to" (from *~gleyb-~, the same root as ~kleben~) and "to split apart" (from *~glewbʰ-~, a different root entirely). These are among the most famous auto-antonyms in English.
en.klettern: An iterative verb formed in Early New High German from ~kletten~, from PIE *~gleyt-~ ("to cling to, cleave, stick"), from the root *~gley-~ ("to stick, smear"). Related to ~Klette~ ("burr") -- the prickly seed casing that clings to clothing and fur -- and, surprisingly, to ~Kleid~ ("dress, garment"), which originally referred to something that clings to the body. The iterative ~-ern~ suffix emphasizes repeated action, capturing the hand-over-hand nature of climbing. The semantic connection between clinging and climbing is vivid: a climber clings to the rock face the way a burr clings to a wool coat.
en.klicken: ~Klicken~ ("to click") is attested from the 16th century, derived from Middle High German *~klicken~, as preserved in ~zerklicken~ ("to break an eggshell"). It is either cognate with or formed in parallel to Dutch ~klikken~ (15th century), English ~click~ (16th century), and French ~cliquer~ (14th century) — all ultimately imitative of the sharp, dry sound a latch, buckle, or button makes. The computing sense — pressing a mouse button — is a 20th-century semantic loan from English ~click~. ~Klicken~ is thus one of the few words in this app to have two distinct origin stories in the same form: an ancient onomatopoeic root and a modern borrowing wearing its face. The verb is wholly regular and weak, befitting something so thoroughly modern.
en.klieben: From MHG ~klieben~, from OHG ~klioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kleuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~kleubaną~, from PIE *~glewbʰ-~ ("to cut, carve"). A class II strong verb (~klieben~, ~klob~, ~gekloben~), though weak forms are now common; the verb is chiefly southern German and Austrian, said of splitting firewood. Cognate with English ~cleave~ ("to split"), Dutch ~klieven~, Old Norse ~kljúfa~. The same PIE root gives Ancient Greek ~glýphein~ ("to carve"), so a split log and a ~hieroglyph~ name the same act.
en.klimmen: From MHG ~klimben~, from OHG ~klimban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klimban~, probably a nasalized variant of Proto-Germanic *~klībaną~ ("to stick, cling"), the root of ~kleben~ — climbing understood as clinging — though that reconstruction is not secure. A class III strong verb (~klimmen~, ~klomm~, ~geklommen~), beside a weak ~klimmte~. Cognate with English ~climb~, which still writes the ~-b-~ that German dropped, Dutch ~klimmen~, Old English ~climban~. Everyday German has ceded the sense to ~klettern~, leaving ~klimmen~ to poetry, to mountains (~erklimmen~) and to the gym (~Klimmzug~, "pull-up").
en.klingen:
From Middle High German ~klingen~, from Old High German ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~. A class III strong verb. Cognate with Middle Dutch ~klinken~, English ~clink~.

The Proto-Germanic root *~klinganą~ is almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin — a phonological icon of the ringing, resonant sound metal makes when struck. English ~clink~ is a direct descendant via Old English *~clincan~. Related by sound-symbolic extension are English ~clang~, ~cling~ (in the sense of a resonant sound), and possibly ~call~. The verb's surviving class III ablaut pattern — ~klingt~/~klang~/~geklungen~ — shows the vowel series (i, a, u) characteristic of Germanic strong verbs with nasal infixes, the same pattern as ~singen~ and ~springen~. German has generalized ~klingen~ from pure sound to metaphorical resonance: a speech can ~klingen wie Musik~, and a name can ~gut klingen~ — uses that extend the root's sonic origin into the domain of general quality or impression.
