This metaphorical extension happened in the 17th century when ~Strahl~ began to describe light and sunbeams, then expanded in the 18th century to water jets (~Wasserstrahl~) and around 1800 to heat (~Wärmestrahlung~, "radiation"). Today ~strahlen~ means both "to radiate/beam" and figuratively "to beam with joy."
en.streben: From Middle High German ~strëben~, from Old High German ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). The verb carries connotations of earnest, directed effort toward a goal. The derived noun ~Streber~ ("overachiever, teacher's pet") has decidedly negative connotations in German, unlike the neutral English ~striver~. The compound ~Bestreben~ ("endeavor") and the participial adjective ~strebsam~ ("ambitious, industrious") maintain more positive associations. Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source related to ~streben~).
en.streichen:
From Middle High German ~strīchen~, from Old High German ~strīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīkaną~ ("to stroke, to rub"), from PIE *~streyg-~ ("to stroke, rub, press"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~strijken~ ("to iron, to stroke"), English ~strike~.

The relationship between ~streichen~ and English ~strike~ is a case study in how cognates can drift apart while remaining connected by a shared core meaning. Both descend from the same Proto-Germanic root meaning "to move in one direction, to rub, to stroke." English ~strike~ hardened the action into a blow; German ~streichen~ softened it into a gliding motion. Modern ~streichen~ means "to stroke, to caress" (~einem Kind über den Kopf streichen~, "to stroke a child's head"), "to spread" (~Butter aufs Brot streichen~, "to spread butter on bread"), "to paint" (~die Wand streichen~, "to paint the wall"), and "to cross out, to cancel, to delete" (~ein Wort streichen~, "to strike out a word"). This last meaning — crossing out — is the closest to English ~strike~ (as in "strike from the record"). In a delightful irony, German borrowed the English cognate back as ~Streik~ ("labor strike") and ~streiken~ ("to go on strike") in the 19th century, because the native ~streichen~ had drifted too far from the combative sense. The noun ~Strich~ ("line, stroke, dash") and the diminutive ~streicheln~ ("to pet, to caress") round out the family.
en.streiten:
From MHG ~strīten~, from OHG ~strītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīdaną~, probably from Pre-Germanic *~streydʰh₁-~, a compound of PIE *~strey-~ ("to resist") + *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, place"). Cognate with Low German ~striden~, Dutch ~strijden~ ("to fight, struggle"), and English ~stride~.

The English cognate ~stride~ reveals a remarkable semantic divergence: while German ~streiten~ means "to quarrel, to argue, to dispute," English ~stride~ means "to walk with long steps." The connection lies in the physical posture of combat -- striding aggressively toward an opponent. Dutch ~strijden~ ("to fight, to battle") preserves the martial sense more faithfully than either German or English. In modern German, ~streiten~ typically refers to verbal conflict (~sich streiten~ = "to argue") rather than physical combat, though the legal compound ~Streit~ ("dispute, lawsuit") maintains a formal register.
en.stärken: ~Stärken~ ("to strengthen") is a denominal verb inherited from Middle High German ~sterken~ and Old High German ~sterken~, formed from the adjective ~stark~ ("strong") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. The adjective ~stark~ and the English adjective ~stark~ are direct cognates, both from Proto-Germanic *~starkuz~ ("stiff, strong"), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)terg-~ ("rigid, stiff"). The semantic split between German and English is a classic false-friend trap: German ~stark~ still means "strong," while English ~stark~ shifted toward "bare, utter, rigid" — as in ~stark naked~ or ~stark raving mad~. English kept the "stiffness" nuance and lost the "strength" nuance. The same root also gives English ~starch~ (via the stiffening property of the substance). So ~stärken~ is cognate with both English ~stark~ and ~starch~, words that feel nothing alike.
en.stören:
From Middle High German ~stören~, from Old High German ~stōren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~staurijan~. Related to Proto-Germanic *~steuran~ and cognate with Dutch ~storen~, Old English ~styrian~ ("to stir, to move, to agitate"), English ~stir~.

The connection between ~stören~ ("to disturb") and English ~stir~ is direct: both descend from the same Germanic root meaning "to move, to agitate." To disturb someone is etymologically to stir them from their rest — to set them in unwanted motion. The derived noun ~Störung~ ("disturbance, malfunction") appears everywhere from psychology (~psychische Störung~, "psychological disorder") to technology (~Netzwerkstörung~, "network disruption"), while the compound ~zerstören~ intensifies the disturbance to total destruction. Cognate with Dutch ~storen~, English ~stir~.
en.stürzen:
From Middle High German ~stürzen~, from Old High German ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin. Possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. Cognate with English ~start~ — a doublet descended from the same Proto-West Germanic source, though the meanings have diverged radically.

The connection between ~stürzen~ ("to fall, to plunge, to overthrow") and English ~start~ ("to begin, to set in motion") is one of the more surprising cognate pairs in Germanic. Both descend from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~, but English preserved the sense of sudden, jerky motion (a startled horse ~starts~), while German kept the sense of precipitous falling. The verb covers an enormous semantic range: intransitively, "to fall, to crash, to plunge, to rush" (~er stürzte vom Dach~, "he fell from the roof"; ~sie stürzte aus dem Zimmer~, "she rushed out of the room"); transitively, "to hurl, to overturn, to overthrow" (~eine Regierung stürzen~, "to overthrow a government"). The reflexive ~sich auf etwas stürzen~ ("to pounce on something, to dive into something") adds eagerness to the violence. The derived noun ~Sturz~ ("fall, plunge, crash") and the compound ~Absturz~ ("crash, precipitous drop") — used equally for aircraft and computer programs — extend the imagery into every domain of German life.
en.stützen: Attested as a simplex verb only since the 17th century. Probably modeled after Middle Low German ~stütten~, as a back-formation from the inherited compound ~unterstützen~, from Middle High German ~understüzzen~, from Old High German ~untarstuzzen~, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *~stuttijan~. The verb is related to Proto-Germanic *~stuþs~ ("post, prop"), whence English ~stud~ (in the architectural sense of "upright post"). Cognate with Dutch ~stutten~ ("to support"), and, through Low German borrowing, Norwegian ~støtte~, Swedish ~stötta~, and probably dialectal English ~stut~ ("to support"). The semantic core of "propping up" has remained remarkably stable across a millennium. In modern German, ~stützen~ covers both physical support ("to brace, to prop") and abstract support ("to back, to substantiate"), a metaphorical extension shared with its English cousin ~support~ (though the two words are unrelated etymologically). The fact that the simplex ~stützen~ is a relatively late back-formation from ~unterstützen~ reverses the usual pattern, where prefixed verbs derive from simpler roots -- here the compound came first.
en.suchen: From Middle High German ~suochen~, ~süechen~, from Old High German ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). The modern form without umlaut reflects the Upper German dialect, which resisted umlaut of long rounded vowels before velars; Central German forms show the expected umlaut (compare Luxembourgish ~sichen~). Cognate with Dutch ~zoeken~, Low German ~söken~, Danish ~søge~, English ~seek~, Gothic ~sōkjan~.
en.tanzen:
From Middle High German ~tanzen~, borrowed via Central German dialects from Old French ~dancier~ (modern French ~danser~). The adapted onset ~t-~ (rather than ~d-~) in Upper German dialects and standard German proves that the word was not borrowed directly from French but entered through Middle Low German or Middle Dutch ~dansen~, passing through Central German before reaching the south, where the High German consonant shift changed ~d-~ to ~t-~.

The ultimate origin of the Old French word is disputed, but it may derive from Frankish *~dansōn~ ("to draw along, to pull"), which would make it a Germanic word that traveled to France with the Franks and then boomeranged back into German. If this Frankish etymology is correct, ~tanzen~ is a remarkable round-trip borrowing: a Germanic word exported to Romance and then re-imported in altered form. English ~dance~ was likewise borrowed from Old French ~dancier~, making ~tanzen~ and ~dance~ doublets of sorts -- both borrowed from the same French source, but through different routes and at different times. The word appears in German texts from around the 12th century, coinciding with the age of courtly ~Minnesang~, when French cultural influence on German aristocratic life was at its peak.
en.tauchen:
From Middle High German ~tūchen~, ~touchen~, from Old High German *~tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, to dive under"). A class II strong verb that became weak during the early modern period. The word had fallen out of use in Upper German dialects but was reintroduced from Central German ~dūchen~/~tūchen~ and Middle Low German ~dūken~, which had remained common. In the course of this revival, the originally strong conjugation was regularized to weak. Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~. A Low German consonant variant of the same root survives as German ~ducken~ ("to duck, to crouch"), cognate with and synonymous with English ~duck~ (the verb).

The etymology of Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ is uncertain. One hypothesis connects it to *~duganą~ ("to be fit, to avail"), suggesting a Pre-Germanic form *~dʰugʰnéh₂-~ with an original meaning of "to fall" that evolved to "to happen, be fitting" (compare ~Zufall~, literally "falling-to," meaning "chance, coincidence"). The transitive sense "to immerse, to submerge, to bathe" (~die Äpfel in heißes Karamell tauchen~, "to dip the apples in hot caramel") coexists with the intransitive "to dive" — a neat semantic pairing of agent and object. The derivative ~auftauchen~ ("to emerge, to surface, to turn up") is among the most common compounds: things, people, and problems all ~tauchen auf~ in German.
en.tauschen:
From Middle High German ~tiuschen~, derived from ~tūschen~, related to ~täuschen~ ("to deceive"), both of uncertain further origin. The semantic shift ran from "to deceive" to "to trick someone into buying one's goods" to "to trade, exchange, barter."

The shared ancestry of ~tauschen~ ("to exchange") and ~täuschen~ ("to deceive") reveals a deeply cynical medieval view of commerce: trading was, at its root, a form of trickery. The two verbs differentiated only gradually, with ~tauschen~ losing its negative connotation while ~täuschen~ retained it. The pair is a classic example of semantic bifurcation, where a single word splits into two with divergent meanings. In modern German, the two words are completely distinct: ~tauschen~ is neutral ("to swap, exchange, barter"), while ~täuschen~ is negative ("to deceive, mislead"). The derivative ~enttäuschen~ ("to disappoint") literally means "to un-deceive" -- to strip away an illusion, revealing a less pleasant reality.
en.teilen: From Middle High German ~teilen~ and Old High German ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~ (alternatively *~dʰayl-~), tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. The semantic core of "dividing into parts" is consistent and stable across the entire recorded history of the word. The same root yields ~Teil~ ("part"), ~Abteil~ ("compartment"), and the legal term ~Anteil~ ("share, stake"). Cognate with Dutch ~delen~, English ~deal~ (in both the commercial sense of "to deal cards / goods" and the older sense of "a part, a great deal"), Danish ~dele~, Swedish ~dela~.
en.testen: Borrowed from English ~test~, plus the German verbal suffix ~-en~. English ~test~ comes from Middle English ~test~, ~teste~, from Old French ~test~, ~teste~ ("an earthen vessel, especially a pot in which metals were tried"), from Latin ~testum~ ("earthen pot, lid of a clay vessel"), related to Latin ~testa~ ("clay pot, potsherd") and ~terra~ ("earth, land"). The leap from clay pot to examination came via assaying: medieval metallurgists placed ore in a ~testum~ to fire and analyze it, and this concrete act of proving metal by heat became the general metaphor for any examination of quality. The word entered German in the twentieth century as a scientific and technical borrowing, making ~testen~ one of the youngest verbs in the standard vocabulary — a word born in the laboratory.
en.tippen: From Low German, where the standard High German equivalent would have been ~tüpfen~ ("to dab, dot"). The word has two distinct semantic branches in modern German. In the sense of "to type" or "to tap," it derives from the onomatopoeic imitation of light touching. In the sense of "to bet, to guess" (as in ~Lotto tippen~), it comes from the noun ~Tipp~, itself borrowed from English ~tip~ ("a piece of advice, a hint"). The coexistence of these two meanings -- tapping keys and placing bets -- makes ~tippen~ a minor source of amusement: ~Ich tippe auf Bayern~ could mean either "I'm typing about Bayern" or "I'm betting on Bayern."
en.tragen: From Middle High German ~tragen~, from Old High German ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with Dutch ~dragen~, English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Danish ~drage~, Icelandic ~draga~, Portuguese ~trazer~.
en.trauen: From Middle High German ~trūwen~, from Old High German ~trūwēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trūwēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~trūwāną~ ("to trust, believe"). The PIE root is *~deru-~ ("to be firm, hard, solid"), which also produced the words for ~tree~ and ~true~ in English, both referring to things that are firm and reliable. The semantic web is stunning: from a single root meaning "solid" grew German ~trauen~ ("to trust"), ~Trost~ ("comfort, consolation"), ~treu~ ("faithful"), and ~Trauung~ ("wedding ceremony," literally an act of entrusting). English ~trust~, ~true~, ~tree~, ~truce~, and ~troth~ all descend from the same PIE root, as do Gothic ~trausti~ ("alliance, pact") and Old Norse ~traust~ ("confidence"). The German verb ~trauen~ has a delightful range: ~ich traue dir~ means "I trust you," ~sich trauen~ means "to dare" (to trust oneself), and ~trauen~ in a church context means "to marry" (to entrust two people to each other). The related ~zutrauen~ means "to believe someone capable of," while ~misstrauen~ means "to distrust." German ~Trost~ and English ~trust~ are doublets from the same Proto-Germanic root *~traustą~.
en.treffen: From Middle High German ~treffen~, from Old High German ~treffan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drepan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drepaną~ ("to strike, push, beat"), from PIE *~dʰrebʰ-~, *~dʰreb-~ ("to crack, crush, strike, kill"). The Proto-Germanic root carried a primary meaning of violent striking — preserved most clearly in Old Norse ~drepa~ ("to kill, strike") and in German ~betreffen~ ("to concern, affect," literally "to strike upon"). Modern German ~treffen~ has largely shed its violent sense, shifting toward "to meet" and "to hit a target," but the original force remains audible in phrases like ~ein Unglück trifft jemanden~ ("a misfortune strikes someone"). The High German consonant shift from *~dr-~ to ~tr-~ obscures the cognate relationship with Old English ~drepan~ ("to strike"). Cognate with Old Norse ~drepa~, Old English ~drepan~.
en.treiben: ~treiben~ comes from Middle High German ~trīben~, from Old High German ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. This is the cognate of English ~drive~: the two words share a Proto-West Germanic ancestor, separated by the High German consonant shift that regularly converted Proto-Germanic *d to German *t. The semantic range in modern German is wide — to drive (animals), to drift (on water), to pursue (a hobby or trade: ~Sport treiben~), to force or compel, and to sprout (~Knospen treiben~) — but all share the underlying sense of impelling motion. Cognate with Dutch ~drijven~, Low German ~drieven~, Swedish ~driva~, and Danish ~drive~. The Class I strong verb ablaut pattern (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) is one of the most regular in the language, directly reflecting the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i.
en.trennen: From Middle High German ~trennen~, from Old High German ~trennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trannijaną~. Cognate with Low German ~trennen~ and Dutch ~tornen~ (archaic ~tarnen~, from Middle Dutch ~ternen~, a metathesis of an older form ~trennen~). The deeper etymology is uncertain; the Proto-Germanic root is not securely connected to any PIE root, and proposed connections to a root meaning "to tear" remain speculative. Dutch ~tornen~ has narrowed to mean specifically "to unpick stitches" — a particularly apt descendant for a verb of separation.
en.treten: From Middle High German ~trëten~, from Old High German ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~. A class V strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~. The Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism: present singular *~tred-~, non-singular *~trud-~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, which may be an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"), related to roots like *~drem-~ ("to run, sleep") and Sanskrit ~drā~ ("to run, make haste"). The semantic shift from "to run" to "to step, tread" reflects a narrowing from general movement to deliberate foot placement. The same Proto-West Germanic base *~tredan~ gives English ~tread~, so the two verbs are direct cognates with essentially the same meaning. Derived forms extend the core sense in vivid directions: ~eintreten~ ("to step in, to occur"), ~auftreten~ ("to appear, perform"), ~betreten~ ("to enter, to step on") — every social entry and stage appearance in German involves the language of footsteps. Cognate with Dutch ~treden~, English ~tread~, Danish ~træde~, Old Norse ~troða~.
en.triefen: From MHG ~triefen~, from OHG ~triufan~, ~triofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dreupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dreupaną~ ("to drip"). Historically a class II strong verb (~triefen~, ~troff~, ~getroffen~), but its strong participle fell together in sound with that of ~treffen~, and a weak ~triefte~, ~getrieft~ took over in the 17th century; ~troff~ now survives only as elevated and dated. Cognate with English ~drip~, ~drop~, and ~droop~, Dutch ~druipen~, Old Norse ~drjúpa~, Old Saxon ~driopan~. The same root gives ~Tropfen~ ("drop") and ~Traufe~ ("eaves"), the latter matching English ~eavesdrop~, which named the strip of ground where roof-water falls before it named the listener standing on it.
en.trinken: ~trinken~ comes from Middle High German ~trinken~, from Old High German ~trinkan~ (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~. This is the same word as English ~drink~: the two are exact cognates separated only by the High German consonant shift, which regularly converted Proto-Germanic *d to German *t (the "dental" portion of the Second Sound Shift). The semantic identity across all Germanic branches is remarkable — Old Saxon ~drinkan~, Old Dutch ~drinkan~, Old English ~drincan~, Old Frisian ~drinka~, Old Norse ~drekka~, and even Gothic ~𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽~ (drigkan) all mean "to drink." No non-Germanic cognate has been securely identified, suggesting the word may be a Germanic innovation, possibly derived from an older root for "drawing liquid." The compound ~ertrinken~ ("to drown") shows how the same root covers both drinking and the lethal overconsumption of water.
en.trocknen: A deadjectival verb from the adjective ~trocken~ ("dry"), formed with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Trocken~ traces to Middle High German ~trucken~, from Old High German ~truckan~, ~trokkan~ ("dried out, parched"), from Proto-West Germanic *~drukn~, from Proto-Germanic *~druknaz~, *~druhnaz~ ("dry"), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰerǵʰ-~ ("to strengthen, become hard or solid"), an extension of *~dʰer-~ ("to hold, hold fast"). The PIE root connects dryness with firmness and solidity, reflecting how drying hardens materials. The form ~trucken~ was originally predominant, but the word eventually standardized with the western variant ~-o-~. Cognate with Old Saxon ~drokno~ ("dry," adverb) and Old English ~gedrycnan~ ("to dry up"). The compound ~Trockenheit~ ("drought, dryness") and ~Wäschetrockner~ ("clothes dryer") are common modern derivatives.
en.träumen:
From Middle High German ~troumen~ and Old High German ~troumen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~draumijan~, a denominative verb from the noun *~draum~ (whence ~Traum~). The noun derives from Proto-Germanic *~draumaz~, from PIE *~dʰrewgʰ-~ ("to deceive, to harm"), suggesting that the ancient Indo-Europeans viewed dreams as fundamentally deceptive experiences. Cognate with Dutch ~dromen~, English ~dream~, and Swedish ~drömma~.

The connection between dreaming and deception runs deep: the PIE root *~dʰrewgʰ-~ also yields Old English ~drēogan~ ("to endure, to suffer") and Sanskrit ~druh-~ ("to harm"). The Germanic ~Traum~/~dream~ words originally may have meant "apparition" or "phantom" rather than the neutral "sleep vision" we intend today. Curiously, Old English ~drēam~ originally meant "joy, music, revelry" -- it only acquired the sense of "sleep vision" in Middle English, possibly under influence from Old Norse ~draumr~. This means German ~Traum~ and English ~dream~ are etymological cognates that arrived at the same meaning through different semantic paths -- German kept the original sense while English took a detour through "music" before circling back.
en.trügen: From MHG ~triegen~, from OHG ~triugan~, ~triogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dreugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dreuganą~ ("to deceive"), from PIE *~dʰrewgʰ-~ ("to deceive, harm"). A class II strong verb (~trügen~, ~trog~, ~getrogen~); the expected modern form would be ~triegen~, and the ~ü~ was taken over by analogy with the rhyming ~lügen~. Cognate with Dutch ~bedriegen~, Old Saxon ~driogan~, and — outside Germanic — Sanskrit ~druhyati~ ("to seek to harm") and Avestan ~druj-~, the name of the Zoroastrian demon of the Lie. One hypothesis traces ~Traum~ and English ~dream~ to the same root, a dream as a phantom that deceives, though the connection is not secure.
en.tätigen:
Derived from the adjective ~tätig~ ("active") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Tätig~ itself derives from the noun ~Tat~ ("deed"), from MHG ~tāt~, OHG ~tāt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dādi~, from Proto-Germanic *~dēdiz~, from PIE *~dʰéh₁-tis~ ("a placing, a doing"), built on the root *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, to place, to do"). This is the same root that gives German ~tun~ ("to do") — so ~Tat~ and ~tun~ are, at the deepest level, the same word. Cognate with Dutch ~daad~, English ~deed~, Danish ~dåd~, Gothic *~dēþs~, Old Norse ~dáð~.

The PIE root *~dʰeh₁-~ is one of the most prolific in the Indo-European family. It produced Greek ~títhēmi~ ("I place"), whence ~thésis~ ("a placing, a proposition") and English ~theme~, ~thesis~, ~apothecary~, and ~thesaurus~ (originally "a storehouse" — a place where things are put). In Latin, the zero-grade *~dʰh₁-~ yielded ~facere~ ("to do, to make") via an Italic sound change, giving English ~fact~, ~factory~, ~faculty~, ~affair~, and ~perfect~ (literally "thoroughly done"). Sanskrit ~dádhāti~ ("he places") shows the reduplicated present that was the original PIE formation.

The verb ~tätigen~ is a relatively modern coinage, attested from the 18th century, and belongs to commercial and legal register: ~einen Kauf tätigen~ ("to make a purchase"), ~eine Investition tätigen~ ("to make an investment"), ~einen Anruf tätigen~ ("to make a call"). In everyday speech, Germans strongly prefer simpler alternatives — ~kaufen~, ~investieren~, ~anrufen~ — making ~tätigen~ a hallmark of bureaucratic German (~Amtsdeutsch~). The journey from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to place") through Germanic ~Tat~ ("deed") to the stiff formality of ~eine Überweisung tätigen~ ("to execute a bank transfer") is a small history of civilization itself: from the concrete act of placing something with one's hands to the abstract machinery of modern commerce.
en.töten:
From Middle High German ~tœten~, ~tœden~, from Old High German *~tōten~, ~tōden~, from Proto-West Germanic *~daudijan~ ("to make dead, to kill"), from Proto-Germanic *~daudijaną~, a factitive (causative) verb derived from *~daudaz~ ("dead") + *~-janą~ (the factitive suffix meaning "to make X"). Cognate with Dutch ~doden~, Old Norse ~deyða~ (Icelandic ~deyða~), Gothic ~dauþjan~. The surface analysis is transparent: ~tot~ ("dead") + ~-en~, literally "to make dead." Compare English ~deaden~, which follows the same derivation pattern from ~dead~ but has a weaker meaning ("to dull, to muffle" rather than "to kill").

The High German consonant shift transformed the initial ~d~ of the Proto-Germanic root to ~t~: *~daudaz~ became OHG ~tōt~, hence ~töten~ rather than the expected *~döden~ (which is precisely the Dutch form: ~doden~). In colloquial German, ~umbringen~ is strongly preferred over ~töten~; the latter sounds clinical and formal, appropriate for news reports (~zehn Menschen wurden getötet~, "ten people were killed") but jarring in everyday speech. The word ~Neuntöter~ ("red-backed shrike," literally "nine-killer") reflects folk belief that this small bird impales nine prey items on thorns before eating — a grisly name for a songbird.
en.wachsen:
From Middle High German ~wahsen~, from Old High German ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb. Cognate with Low German ~wassen~, Dutch ~wassen~, West Frisian ~waakse~, English ~wax~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~. Non-Germanic cognates include Ancient Greek ~aéxein~ ("to increase") and Latin ~auxilium~ ("help," from a sense of "increase of strength").

English preserves the same verb as the literary and poetic ~wax~ ("the moon waxes"), enshrined in the phrase ~wax and wane~. In everyday modern English the verb ~wax~ (to grow) is archaic except in that fixed phrase and in expressions like "to wax poetic." German ~wachsen~ has remained the ordinary word for growing throughout — of plants, of children, of economies. The PIE root *~h₂weg-~ is also the ancestor of Latin ~augēre~ ("to increase"), giving English ~augment~, ~auction~ (from "increase by bidding"), and the imperial title ~Augustus~ ("the increased, the revered one"). The ablaut series ~wächst~/~wuchs~/~gewachsen~ follows class VI. The compound ~entwachsen~ ("to outgrow") and the noun ~Wuchs~ ("growth, stature") preserve the root's productive legacy.
en.wagen: From Middle High German ~wāgen~ ("to risk, to dare"), ultimately derived from Old High German ~wāga~ ("scales, balance; weight") — the modern word ~Waage~ ("scales"). The underlying metaphor is vivid: to ~wagen~ is to place something on the scales without knowing where the balance will fall. The OHG noun ~wāga~ descends from Proto-West Germanic *~wāgu~ ("scales"), from Proto-Germanic *~wēgō~, related to *~weganą~ ("to move, to weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to move, to transport, to carry"). This root is spectacularly productive: it gave Latin ~vehere~ ("to carry") and its derivatives ~vehicle~, ~convex~, ~invective~; English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~ ("wagon"); and German ~Weg~ ("way"), ~bewegen~ ("to move"), ~wiegen~ ("to weigh"), and ~Wagen~ ("car, wagon"). The noun ~Wagen~ and the verb ~wagen~ are thus false friends in disguise: ~Wagen~ comes from the "vehicle" branch of the root, while ~wagen~ comes from the "scales" branch — yet both trace back to the same PIE notion of weighing and moving. Cognate with Dutch ~wagen~ ("to dare").
en.wandeln:
From Middle High German ~wandeln~, from Old High German ~wantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with Dutch ~wandelen~ ("to walk, stroll"), English ~wend~ (from OE ~wendan~, "to turn"), and ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil").

~Wandeln~ means both "to walk, to stroll" (an elevated, literary synonym for ~gehen~) and "to change, to transform" (~sich wandeln~). These senses seem unrelated, but both descend from the root idea of turning: to walk is to turn one's steps in a direction, and to change is to turn into something else. The same dual meaning survives in the related noun ~Wandel~ ("change, transformation") and the famous compound ~Wanderlust~, which passed into English unchanged. The tribal name ~Vandals~ (~Wandali~) may derive from the same root, possibly meaning "the wanderers."
en.wandern: From Middle High German ~wandern~, from Old High German *~wantarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandarōn~, itself formed from *~wandōn~ ("to turn, to change") with the frequentative suffix *~-rōn~, suggesting repeated or habitual turning or moving about. The root traces to Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~ ("to turn"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). The frequentative formation captures the essential nature of wandering: not a single purposeful journey but a repeated, meandering motion. The word is attested since the 13th century and originally carried the sense of journeying on foot as a tradesman — the ~Wanderjahre~ ("years of wandering") were the years a journeyman spent traveling from workshop to workshop after completing his apprenticeship, a tradition formalized in the medieval guild system and still practiced by some German tradespeople today. Cognate with English ~wander~ (from the same Proto-West Germanic source), Dutch ~wandelen~ ("to stroll, to walk for pleasure"), Danish ~vandre~, Swedish ~vandra~. The PIE root *~wendʰ-~ also gives English ~wind~ (the verb, "to twist") and ~wend~, German ~wenden~ ("to turn"), and Latin ~ventus~ ("wind" — air that turns and twists). The cultural concept of ~Wanderlust~ — that restless longing for the open road — was borrowed into English directly from German, one of those rare words that filled a gap no English term could.
en.warnen: From Middle High German ~warnen~ ("to watch over, to protect"), from Old High German ~warnōn~ ("to deny, to refuse, to decline"), from Proto-West Germanic *~warnōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~warnōną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, to perceive, to watch out for"). The semantic evolution is noteworthy: in Old High German, ~warnōn~ meant "to refuse, to deny" — an act of self-protection. By Middle High German, the sense had shifted to "to watch over, to guard, to caution" — protecting others rather than oneself. In Modern German, ~warnen~ means specifically "to warn, to caution" (~vor etwas warnen~, "to warn against something"). The shift from refusal to warning follows a natural logic: one who refuses danger for oneself eventually tells others to do the same. Cognate with Old English ~wyrnan~ ("to refuse, to withhold"), Old Norse ~varna~ ("to refuse"), Old Saxon ~wernian~ ("to decline, to withhold"), and — most strikingly — English ~warn~, which underwent the same semantic shift independently. The PIE root *~wer-~ also yields Latin ~verēri~ ("to fear, to respect," whence English ~revere~), German ~wahren~ ("to safeguard"), and ~Wart~ ("watchman," as in ~Torwart~, "goalkeeper"). The derived noun ~Warnung~ ("warning") and the ~Warnweste~ ("high-visibility vest") both preserve the ancient watching-over sense.
en.warten:
From Middle High German ~warten~, from Old High German ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, protect, watch over"), derived from *~warduz~ ("a guard"), ultimately from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard").

The semantic shift from "to guard, watch over" to "to wait" reflects the experience of a sentinel: one who keeps watch necessarily also waits. This same shift occurred in English ~ward~ (from the same root) and in French ~garder~ ("to guard") and ~attendre~ ("to wait," literally "to attend to"). In Modern German, ~warten~ retains both senses in certain contexts — ~warte auf mich~ ("wait for me") and the older sense of tending/caring persists in ~warten~ as "to service, maintain" (as in ~ein Auto warten~, "to service a car"), a usage that connects back directly to the original "to watch over, tend." Cognate with Old Saxon ~wardōn~, Swedish ~vårda~ ("to tend, care for"), English ~ward~, Dutch ~bewaren~ ("to keep, preserve").
en.waschen:
From Middle High German ~waschen~, from Old High German ~wascan~, ~waskan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~ ("to wash"), from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"). The same PIE root gives English ~water~, ~wet~, and ~wash~ itself. Cognate with Dutch ~wassen~, English ~wash~, West Frisian ~waskje~, Danish ~vaske~.

The PIE derivation is revealing: ~waschen~ is built on a present-tense formation with the ~ske~-suffix (PIE *~wod-ske-~), a morphological pattern used to create iterative or inchoative presents. The basic meaning was "to make wet (repeatedly)" — washing as the iterative application of water. German ~waschen~ and English ~wash~ descend from the same Proto-Germanic word and have maintained nearly identical meanings across a millennium of independent development. The verb is also notable as an anagram of ~wachsen~ ("to grow") — a coincidence with no etymological significance but one that generations of German schoolchildren have noticed. The reflexive ~sich die Hände waschen~ ("to wash one's hands") carries the same metaphorical meaning of moral disavowal as in English, both ultimately from the biblical account of Pontius Pilate.
en.weben: From MHG ~weben~, from OHG ~weban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~weban~, from Proto-Germanic *~webaną~, from PIE *~webʰ-~ ("to weave, braid"). Originally a class V strong verb (OHG ~weban~, ~wab~, ~giweban~); modern German conjugates it weak (~webte~, ~gewebt~) for the literal craft, while the strong ~wob~, ~gewoben~ — whose ~o~ is a later analogical remodelling on the pattern of ~heben~, ~hob~, ~gehoben~ — belongs to elevated and figurative use (~um ihn wob sich eine Legende~). Cognate with English ~weave~ and ~web~, Dutch ~weven~, Danish ~væve~, Ancient Greek ~ὑφαίνω~ (hyphaínō, "I weave"). ~Wabe~ ("honeycomb") belongs to the same root as a thing woven, and by way of Dutch ~wafel~ it is the ancestor of English ~waffle~.
en.wechseln:
From Middle High German ~wëhseln~, from Old High German *~wehsalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wihslōną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ ("to change, bend, yield"). Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, Luxembourgish ~wiesselen~, Latin ~vicis~ ("change, turn, alternation"), English ~week~, German ~Woche~.

The connection between ~wechseln~ and English ~week~ runs through the Proto-Germanic root *~wikǭ~ ("sequence, turn"), itself from *~wīkaną~ ("to bend, yield, give way"). A week is a "turn" of days, a cycle that yields to the next. The same root produced Latin ~vicis~ ("change, alternation, turn") — found in ~vice versa~ ("with the turn reversed"), ~vicar~ (one who stands in another's turn or place), and ~vicious~ (originally relating to a flaw in the pattern). German ~Woche~ and English ~week~ are thus cognates of ~wechseln~, all sharing the sense of something that changes, turns, or yields its place. The notion of currency exchange (~Geldwechsel~) preserves the oldest concrete sense: money, like days, passes from hand to hand in alternating turns. Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, English ~week~, Latin ~vicis~ ("turn, change").
en.wecken:
From Middle High German ~wecken~, from Old High German ~wecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wakkjan~ ("to wake up, to awaken"), from Proto-Germanic *~wakjaną~, a causative formation from *~wakaną~ ("to be awake"), from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, to wake"). The causative relationship is transparent: *~wakaną~ means "to be awake" (intransitive), *~wakjaną~ means "to make awake" (transitive) — and this is precisely the modern German distinction between ~wachen~ ("to be awake, to keep watch") and ~wecken~ ("to wake someone up"). Cognate with Dutch ~wekken~, English ~watch~ (from the same Proto-West Germanic source but with a different semantic development).

The English cognate ~watch~ reveals a surprising semantic drift: from "to wake, to be alert" (Old English ~wæccan~) to "to observe attentively" to "a timepiece used to mark the hours of wakefulness." German ~wecken~ stayed closer to the original causative meaning. The derived noun ~Wecker~ ("alarm clock") is transparently "the thing that wakes you" — a straightforward agent noun. The compound ~aufwecken~ ("to wake up," with emphasis on the completion of the action) adds the ~auf-~ prefix for thoroughness. The related word ~erwecken~ ("to awaken, to arouse") has developed a strong figurative and religious sense: ~Erweckung~ ("awakening, revival") refers to spiritual renewal, as in the ~Erweckungsbewegung~ ("revival movement").
en.wehren:
From MHG ~weren~, from OHG ~werien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~warjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~ ("to defend, to ward off, to protect"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to close, to cover, to protect"). Cognate with English ~weir~ (a defensive barrier across a stream), ~ward~, ~warden~, ~guard~ (via Old French, from Frankish *~wardōn~), Dutch ~weren~, Old Norse ~verja~, Gothic ~warjan~.

~Wehren~ means "to defend, to ward off" and is most commonly used reflexively: ~sich wehren~ ("to defend oneself, to resist"). The noun ~Wehr~ gives rise to ~Bundeswehr~ ("Federal Defense" — Germany's armed forces), ~Feuerwehr~ ("fire defense" — the fire department), and ~Wehrmacht~ ("defense force" — the name of Germany's armed forces from 1935 to 1945). The PIE root *~wer-~ ("to close, to cover, to protect") is enormously productive: it yielded Latin ~aperīre~ ("to open" — literally "to un-cover," with privative ~a-~), whence English ~aperture~; Latin ~operīre~ ("to cover"), whence ~cover~ itself (via Old French); and Sanskrit ~vr̥ṇóti~ ("he covers, he closes"). The English words ~warn~, ~warrant~, ~garrison~, and ~guarantee~ all trace back through different paths to this same defensive root.
en.weichen:
From Middle High German ~wīchen~, from Old High German ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~ ("to yield, give way"), Old Norse ~vīkja~ ("to turn, retreat"), Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").

~Weichen~ means "to yield, to give way, to retreat." It is not to be confused with the weak verb ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from a different source (~weich~ "soft"). The strong verb's PIE root *~h₃weyg-~ is also the ancestor of Old Norse ~vík~ ("bay, inlet" -- a place where the coastline bends), which gave us the word ~Viking~: people of the inlets, or perhaps people who turn aside (i.e., raiders who venture out). The connection between yielding and bending is preserved in the cognate Swedish ~vika~, which means both "to yield" and "to fold."
en.weinen:
From Middle High German ~weinen~, from Old High German ~weinōn~ ("to cry, lament, cry woe"), from Proto-Germanic *~wainōną~ ("to wail, weep"), from PIE *~wáy~ ("woe!"). Cognate with Gothic ~wainon~ ("to suffer"), Old Norse ~veina~ ("to wail"), Old English ~wānian~ ("to bewail"), and Dutch ~wenen~ ("to weep, to cry"). Related to ~Weh~ ("woe, pain"), from Proto-Germanic *~waiwô~, from the same exclamatory root.

The connection between ~weinen~ and English ~woe~ reveals that both descend from what was originally an exclamation of grief — a raw sound of pain that became grammaticalized into a verb ("to express woe") and a noun ("the state of grief"). The PIE exclamation *~wáy~ also produced Latin ~vae~ ("woe!," as in ~vae victis~ "woe to the vanquished") and Old Irish ~fáe~ ("woe"). The German noun ~Wein~ ("wine") is an unrelated homograph, borrowed from Latin ~vīnum~ — a false-friend trap that has confused many a beginning German student. The distinction between ~weinen~ ("to cry, to weep") and ~heulen~ ("to howl, to bawl") mirrors the ~lächeln~/~lachen~ pair in reverse: ~weinen~ is dignified, quiet grief, while ~heulen~ is loud and unrestrained.
en.weisen:
From Middle High German ~wīsen~, from Old High German ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb derived from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb.

The PIE root *~weyd-~ ("to see, know") is one of the most productive in the entire Indo-European family. It yields Latin ~videō~ ("I see"), Sanskrit ~veda~ ("I know"), and Ancient Greek ~eídō~ ("I see; I know"). In Germanic, the root produced both ~wissen~ ("to know") — a preterite-present verb — and the adjective ~weise~ ("wise"), whence ~weisen~. English ~wise~, ~wit~, and ~wizard~ all derive from the same PIE root, as does English ~vision~ (via Latin ~vidēre~). The two modern German senses of ~weisen~ — "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" (as in ~ausweisen~, "to expel or identify," and ~verweisen~, "to refer or rebuke") — both flow from the underlying idea of directing knowledge or attention: to point is to make someone see, and to expel is to direct away. The noun ~Beweis~ ("proof, evidence") is a nominalization of the same root, preserving the ancient link between seeing and knowing.
en.wenden: From Middle High German ~wenden~, from Old High German ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from Proto-Indo-European *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). English ~wend~ is a direct cognate, surviving in the fixed phrase "to wend one's way." Old English ~wendan~ ("to turn, go") gave Middle English ~wenden~ before it was gradually displaced by ~go~; only the idiom "wend one's way" endures. The causative relationship between *~windaną~ and *~wandijaną~ is the same pattern seen in German ~winden~ ("to wind") and ~wenden~ ("to turn something") — the a-grade vowel in ~wenden~ is the Indo-European causative ablaut grade, meaning "to cause to wind." Armenian ~gind~ ("ring") is a non-Germanic cognate preserving the original sense of circular turning. ~Wenden~ belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~), in which the preterite does not carry umlaut (see ~brennen~ for the phonological explanation). Like ~senden~, it has a doubled preterite: the historically strong form ~wandte~ is preferred today for turning the self or one's attention (~sich an jemanden wenden~ "to address someone," ~sich abwenden~ "to turn away"), while the regularized ~wendete~ is preferred for physical turning (~das Auto wendete~ "the car turned around").
en.werben: From Middle High German ~werben~, from Old High German ~werban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hwerban~, from Proto-Germanic *~hwerbaną~ ("to turn, move about, wander"). Cognate with Dutch ~werven~ ("to recruit"), English ~wharve~ ("to turn"), and Icelandic ~hverfa~ ("to turn, disappear"). The semantic evolution from "to turn, move about" to "to recruit, advertise, woo" followed a path through "to be busy, to go about doing something" to "to go about seeking" and finally "to solicit." This is remarkably parallel to the English word ~advertise~, which comes from Latin ~advertere~ ("to turn toward"). Both languages independently linked the concept of turning with the act of seeking attention. The related noun ~Werbung~ ("advertising") is ubiquitous in modern German, and ~Bewerber~ ("applicant") preserves the old sense of one who "goes about" seeking a position. English ~wharf~ is a distant cousin, from Old English ~hwearf~ ("heap, embankment"), related to the same root via the notion of a turning-place for ships. The Faroese cognate ~hvørva~ ("to disappear") preserves yet another semantic branch: turning away until one vanishes.
en.werfen:
From Middle High German ~wërfen~, from Old High German ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb. Cognate with Old Saxon ~werpan~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~, and English ~warp~.

The PIE root *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp") reflects the original sense of a rotational or twisting motion — the physical action of winding up before releasing a projectile. English ~warp~ preserves the root in a different semantic branch: the ~warp~ of a loom is the set of threads stretched lengthwise under tension, and the verb "to warp" means to bend or twist out of shape. German ~werfen~ has developed an exceptionally wide range of compound and idiomatic uses: ~verwerfen~ ("to reject," literally "to throw away"), ~entwerfen~ ("to design, draft," literally "to throw out a plan"), ~einwerfen~ ("to throw in, interject"), and the noun ~Wurf~ ("throw, litter of animals"). The ablaut series ~wirft~/~warf~/~geworfen~ follows the class III pattern shared with ~sterben~.
en.werten:
Derived from ~Wert~ ("value, worth"). ~Wert~ descends from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worth, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"), related to Latin ~versus~ ("turned") and English ~worth~. The modern spelling with ~-t~ (rather than historical ~-d~) was generalized from the uninflected form.

~Werten~ means "to evaluate, to rate, to judge the value of" — a denominal verb transparently formed from ~Wert~. It is common in sports commentary (~Die Jury wertet die Leistung~, "The judges rate the performance"), academic contexts, and legal language. The deeper etymology is striking: PIE *~wert-~ meant "to turn," and the connection to value is through the concept of exchange — turning goods over in a transaction. This same root produced Latin ~vertere~ ("to turn"), whence English ~verse~, ~version~, ~convert~, and ~controversy~. The Germanic branch took the "exchange" sense and solidified it into "worth" — what something is valued at when turned over in trade. English ~worth~, ~worthy~, and ~worship~ (originally "worthship") all descend from this root.
en.wiegen:
German has two distinct verbs spelled ~wiegen~, both from Middle High German ~wigen~:

Sense 1 ("to weigh"): From MHG ~wigen~, a northwestern variant of ~wegen~, which generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~ (from MHG ~wige~, ~wiges~, ~wiget~) across the whole paradigm. From OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"). Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~, Icelandic ~vega~. The original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~, now restricted to figurative senses and derivatives like ~abwägen~ ("to weigh up") and ~erwägen~ ("to consider").

Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): From MHG ~wigen~, derived from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, ~wiega~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ (the same root as sense 1). The connection is movement: weighing involves the motion of a balance, and rocking involves the swaying of a cradle.

Both senses thus trace back to the same PIE notion of movement, though they arrived at their modern meanings by different paths. The PIE root *~weǵʰ-~ also gave Latin ~vehere~ ("to carry"), source of English ~vehicle~, ~vector~, and ~convey~.
en.winden: From MHG ~winden~, from OHG ~wintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~windaną~ ("to wind, to wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with English ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil"), Dutch ~winden~, Danish ~vinde~.
en.winken: From MHG ~winken~, from OHG ~winken~ ("to nod, to blink"), from Proto-West Germanic *~winkōn~ (beside *~winkijan~), from PIE *~weng-~ ("to bend, to curve") — the same root as ~Winkel~ ("angle, corner") and, in ablaut, ~wanken~ ("to sway"). A weak verb, and already weak in OHG. Cognate with English ~wink~, Dutch ~wenken~, and, through the sense "bent thing," English ~winch~. The strong participle ~gewunken~ is a latecomer rather than a survival: Upper German dialects built strong forms on the model of ~sinken~/~gesunken~ in the MHG period, and over the last century ~gewunken~ has pushed the historically regular ~gewinkt~ toward the margins.
en.wirken: From Middle High German ~wirken~, from Old High German ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, derived from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from PIE *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). This root also yields the English noun ~work~ and, via Greek ~ἔργον~ ("work", the direct reflex of PIE *~wérǵom~), the English loanword ~energy~. Early on, ~wirken~ merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~, PWGmc *~wurkijan~, PGmc *~wurkijaną~, a closely related form); the ~i~-form prevailed in Central German, the ~ü~-form in Upper German, with the ~ü~-form displaced from the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~ (the archaic past tense of ~work~, from the same PGmc *~wurkijaną~), Dutch ~werken~.
en.wohnen:
From Middle High German ~wonen~, from Old High German ~wonēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wunēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunāną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love, strive for"). Cognate with Dutch ~wonen~, English ~wont~ ("accustomed"), Old English ~ġewunian~ ("to be accustomed to, dwell").

The PIE root *~wenh₁-~ connects dwelling with desiring: to inhabit a place is to love it enough to remain. The same root underlies German ~Wonne~ ("bliss, rapture"), ~wünschen~ ("to wish"), and ~gewinnen~ ("to win, gain") — in each case, the core sense is striving toward what one loves or desires. English ~wont~ (as in "as was his wont") descends from Old English ~ġewunian~ ("to be accustomed to, dwell"), the same verb as Proto-West Germanic *~wunēn~: to be ~wont~ is to be "dwelt," habituated into a place or practice. English ~win~ (from the same *~wenh₁-~ root via *~winnaną~) preserves the striving sense — to win was originally to labor, struggle toward the desired goal, not merely to come first. The cluster of ~wohnen~, ~Wonne~, ~wünschen~, ~gewinnen~, and English ~wont~ and ~win~ all radiate from the same ancient notion: the thing you love enough to reach for, dwell in, or be shaped by. Cognate with Dutch ~wonen~, Afrikaans ~woon~, English ~wont~, Gothic ~wunan~.
en.wringen: Borrowed into standard German from Low German ~wringen~, from Middle Low German ~wringen~, from Old Saxon ~wringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wringaną~, from PIE *~wrengʰ-~ ("to turn, to twist"), a nasalized extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn, to bend"). A class III strong verb (~wringen~, ~wrang~, ~gewrungen~). Cognate with English ~wring~, Old English ~wringan~, Dutch ~wringen~; the inherited High German reflex of the very same verb is ~ringen~, which lost its initial ~w-~ before ~r~ and moved from "twist" to "wrestle, struggle" — the older sense survives in ~die Hände ringen~ ("to wring one's hands"). English ~wrong~ belongs to the same family by way of Old Norse ~rangr~ ("crooked, twisted"): what is wrong is what has been wrung out of true.
en.wundern:
From Middle High German ~wundern~, from Old High German ~wuntarōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundrōną~, derived from the noun *~wundrą~ ("wonder, miracle"), whence German ~Wunder~. The noun *~wundrą~ may derive from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to desire, wish for, strive after, win, love") via a form *~wn̥h₁-tro-m~, suggesting the original sense was something "wished for" or "longed for" -- hence marvellous.

The verb's reflexive usage, ~sich wundern~ ("to be surprised, to wonder"), is the most common in modern German. The non-reflexive transitive ~das wundert mich~ ("that surprises me") places the wondering person as the object, not the subject -- a grammatical pattern shared by several German verbs of emotion (~freuen~, ~ärgern~, ~langweilen~). English ~wonder~ is not a direct cognate; it derives from Old English ~wundrian~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundrōną~, making it in fact a sibling -- both descend from the same Proto-Germanic verb, though their respective noun bases (~Wunder~ vs. ~wonder~) diverged phonetically through the High German consonant shift.
en.wägen: From MHG ~wegen~ ("to set in motion, to weigh, to be worth"), from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, to move"). A class V strong verb whose modern principal parts are ~wägen~, ~wog~, ~gewogen~ (rarely weak ~wägte~, ~gewägt~), the ~o~-vocalism having prevailed from the fifteenth century onward. It is the doublet of ~wiegen~, which generalized the ~i~ of the old present singular and took over the literal business of weighing, leaving ~wägen~ the figurative one, chiefly in ~abwägen~ ("to weigh up") and ~erwägen~ ("to consider"). The ~ä~ spelling is a seventeenth-century refashioning after ~Waage~ ("scales"); the same PIE root gave ~Weg~, ~Wagen~, English ~way~, ~weigh~, and ~wain~, and Latin ~vehere~ ("to carry"), source of ~vehicle~.
en.wählen: From Middle High German ~weln~, from ~welen~, ~wellen~, from Old High German ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, ultimately from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The modern umlaut vowel ~ä~ developed from the influence of the second- and third-person singular forms in Middle High German. As the ~wollen~ entry notes, ~wählen~ and ~wollen~ share the same PIE root — an elegant reminder that willing and choosing were once a single concept in Proto-Indo-European. Cognate with English ~well~ (in the archaic sense "to wish well"), Dutch ~willen~ (from the same root via a parallel path).
en.währen:
From Middle High German ~wëren~, ~wërn~, from Old High German ~wërēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~weʀēn~, related to OHG ~wesen~ ("to be, exist"). The deeper connection runs through Proto-Germanic *~wēraz~ ("true"), from PIE *~weh₁ros~ ("true"), from *~weh₁-~ ("true, trustworthy").

The semantic thread connecting "to last, endure" with "true" is the idea that what is true is what stands firm and persists. This same root gave German ~wahr~ ("true"), ~Wahrheit~ ("truth"), and the now-archaic ~Wesen~ ("being, essence"). The famous German proverb ~Was lange währt, wird endlich gut~ ("What lasts long turns out good in the end") captures the verb's core meaning. Latin ~vērus~ ("true"), Irish ~fíor~ ("true"), and Slavic *~vě̀ra~ ("faith") are all cognates from the same PIE root, showing that the ancient link between duration and truth runs across the entire Indo-European family.
en.wünschen: From Middle High German ~wünschen~, ~wunschen~, from Old High German ~wunsken~ ("to choose, wish, desire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wunskijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunskijaną~, derived from *~wunskaz~ ("wish, desire"), from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love"). The same PIE root underlies German ~Wonne~ ("bliss, rapture") and English ~win~ — both preserving the old sense of "desired thing, pleasure." The connection between wishing and winning reflects a Proto-Germanic world in which what one wished for was what one strove to obtain. Cognate with Dutch ~wensen~, English ~wish~, Danish ~ønske~, and — across a vast linguistic distance — Sanskrit ~vāṃchati~ ("to wish, desire").
en.würdigen:
From ~würdig~ ("worthy") + ~-en~. ~Würdig~ derives from ~Würde~ ("dignity, worth") + ~-ig~. ~Würde~ descends from MHG ~wirde~, from OHG ~wirdī~, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("valuable, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"). Cognate with English ~worth~ and ~worthy~.

~Würdigen~ means "to honor, to appreciate, to acknowledge the worth of" -- and, in a less common construction, ~keines Blickes würdigen~ ("to not deem worthy of a single glance"), which expresses withering contempt. The PIE root *~wert-~ ("to turn") connects ~Würde~ to Latin ~vertere~ ("to turn"), whence English ~convert~, ~divert~, and ~versus~; the Germanic branch produced ~werden~ ("to become," literally "to turn into"), ~-wärts~ ("-ward," as in ~vorwärts~), and English ~worth~. The development from "turning" to "exchanging" to "having value" to "being worthy" to "dignity" traces a beautiful arc across five millennia of semantic evolution.
en.zahlen:
From Middle High German ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from Old High German ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). Cognate with Bavarian ~zoin~, Dutch ~talen~, Swedish ~tala~, English ~tale~.

~Zahlen~ ("to pay") and ~zählen~ ("to count") are siblings from the same Proto-Germanic root *~talōną~. This root carried both counting and narrating from the beginning — a duality visible in English ~tell~ (to count: ~teller~ at a bank, ~telling beads~; to narrate: to tell a story) and ~tale~ (a story, but also archaic "a count, tally"). The semantic path from "to count" to "to pay" is natural: payment requires counting out the correct amount. In medieval German, ~zalen~ meant both to count and to pay, and the modern distinction between ~zahlen~ and ~zählen~ reflects the same productive split that gave English ~tell~ and ~tale~ their divergent senses. Cognate with Dutch ~betalen~ (via the same root), English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Danish ~tale~ ("to speak"), Swedish ~tala~ ("to speak").
en.zaubern:
From Middle High German ~zoubern~, from Old High German ~zouberōn~, ~zoubarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taubrōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taubrōną~, derived from *~taubrą~ ("magic, sorcery"). Cognate with English ~tiver~ (a red pigment, perhaps originally used in magical rituals) and Dutch ~toveren~ ("to do magic"), Old Norse ~taufr~ ("magic, sorcery").

The origin of Proto-Germanic *~taubrą~ is uncertain, but it may be linked to *~tawjaną~ ("to make, prepare"), suggesting that magic was originally understood as a kind of crafting or making. The Gothic Bible translator Wulfila used ~taujan~ for "to do, make," and the idea of magic as fabrication -- making something appear from nothing -- fits this connection. The noun ~Zauber~ ("magic, spell") and the fairy-tale figure ~Zauberer~ ("wizard, sorcerer") both stem from this root. Interestingly, the old Germanic word for magic survived where many other pagan-era terms did not, resisting replacement by Latin or Christian vocabulary.
en.zeichnen: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from Middle High German ~zeichen~, from Old High German ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"). Cognate with Dutch ~teken~, English ~token~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~. The PIE root *~deyḱ-~ is extraordinarily productive: it also underlies German ~zeigen~ ("to show"), Latin ~dīcere~ ("to say," giving English ~dictate~, ~judge~, ~index~), Greek ~deiknynai~ ("to show"), and Sanskrit ~diś-~ ("direction"). To draw (~zeichnen~) is etymologically to make a sign — and the sign itself descends from the same ancestral root as the act of pointing and showing. English ~token~ and German ~Zeichen~ are cognates across a millennium of linguistic divergence: both mean "a sign left behind to be read."
en.zeigen: From Middle High German ~zeigen~, from Old High German ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, possibly from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~ (an iterative formation). An intensive derivative of Old High German ~zīhan~ ("to accuse"), whence modern ~zeihen~ ("to blame"). Ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"), whence also ~Zeichen~ ("sign") and English ~teach~. In Modern German, ~zeigen~ absorbed the synonymous but entirely unrelated Middle High German ~zöugen~ (cognate with Gothic ~ataugjan~).
en.zeihen: From OHG ~zīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~tīhaną~ ("to show, point out; to blame, accuse"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show"). Cognate with Latin ~dīcō~ ("to speak, say"), Ancient Greek ~δείκνυμι~ (~deíknumi~, "to show, point out"), and English ~token~ (from the related *~taikną~, "sign").
en.zeugen:
From Middle High German ~ziugen~, ~geziugen~, from Old High German ~giziugon~, from ~ziug~ ("equipment, gear"), ultimately from the root of ~ziehen~ ("to pull, draw, move"). The underlying noun ~Zeug~ comes from MHG ~ziuc~ ("stuff, gear"), from OHG ~giziug~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teug~, from Proto-Germanic *~teugą~, related to *~teuhaną~ ("to pull"), from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead").

The original meaning of ~zeugen~ was "to produce, bring forth through technical activity" -- literally to pull something into existence using tools (~Zeug~). From this developed two distinct modern senses: "to beget, procreate" (producing a child) and "to testify, bear witness" (producing evidence). The noun ~Zeuge~ ("witness") comes from the verb, as does ~Zeugnis~ ("testimony, certificate"). English ~tug~ descends from the same PIE root *~dewk-~. Cognate with Dutch ~tuig~ ("equipment, gear"), Old Norse ~tygi~ ("gear"). The semantic range of ~zeugen~ -- from making things, to making children, to making a case in court -- is a remarkable study in conceptual extension.
en.ziehen: From Middle High German ~ziehen~, from Old High German ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Low German ~tehn~, Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~. Cognate with obsolete English ~tee~ ("to draw, lead, proceed") and English ~tie~, from the same PIE root.
en.zielen:
From ~Ziel~ ("target, goal") + ~-en~. ~Ziel~ descends from MHG ~zil~, from OHG ~zil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~til~, from Proto-Germanic *~tilą~ ("aim, goal, fixed point"). Cognate with Old English ~til~ ("suitable, fitting"), whence English ~till~ (preposition: "up to a fixed point").

~Zielen~ means "to aim" — both physically (~auf ein Ziel zielen~, "to aim at a target") and figuratively (~auf etwas zielen~, "to be directed at something"). The verb is a relatively transparent denominal formation: to aim is to direct oneself toward a fixed point (~Ziel~). The Proto-Germanic *~tilą~ connects to a semantic field of fitness and suitability rather than spatial targets — Old English ~til~ meant "suitable, good, apt," and the preposition ~till~ ("up to") preserves the sense of reaching a fixed endpoint. German ~Ziel~ narrowed to the spatial and aspirational senses: the place you aim for, the goal you strive toward. The noun ~Zielscheibe~ ("target disc") makes the archery metaphor explicit, while ~Ziellinie~ ("finish line") extends it to racing.
en.zwingen:
From Middle High German ~twingen~, from Old High German ~dwingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwinganą~, *~þwinhaną~. What appears to be a triple consonant shift (Germanic *~þ~ to OHG ~d~ to MHG ~t~ to modern ~z~) is actually a regular development that affected most words with OHG ~dw-~ and ~tw-~, compare ~Zwerg~ ("dwarf"). A class III strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~zwingen~, ~zwang~, ~gezwungen~. Cognate with Dutch ~dwingen~, Norwegian ~tvinge~, Swedish ~tvinga~, Icelandic ~þvinga~, and English ~twinge~.

The English cognate ~twinge~ — a sharp, sudden pain that grips or squeezes — preserves the original physical sense of the Proto-Germanic verb: to press, to squeeze, to constrain. German ~zwingen~ elevated this physical compression into abstract compulsion: "to force, to compel, to make someone do something." The noun ~Zwang~ ("compulsion, coercion") and the adjective ~zwingend~ ("compelling, cogent") carry the same force. The medieval ~Zwinger~ — the narrow space between inner and outer castle walls where attackers were "squeezed" and trapped — survives today as the name of Dresden's famous ~Zwinger~ palace complex, built on the site of such a fortification.
en.zählen:
From Middle High German ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from Old High German ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). The modern long vowel continues the second- and third-person singular of the present (where West Germanic gemination did not occur); it was reinforced by the lengthened vowel in ~Zahl~ (from MHG ~zale~, "number").

The Proto-Germanic root *~taljaną~ carried both senses — "to count" and "to recount, narrate" — from the very beginning. Modern German split these into two verbs: ~zählen~ retained "to count," while ~erzählen~ (via the ~er-~ prefix) specialized in "to narrate." English underwent the same bifurcation: ~tell~ (from the same root) means both "to count" (as in ~teller~ at a bank, or ~telling beads~) and "to narrate." The word ~tale~ ("a story" but also archaic "a count, tally") shares this dual heritage. Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
en.ändern: From Middle High German ~endern~, a denominative verb derived from ~ander~ ("other, different"). ~Ander~ descends from MHG ~ander~, from OHG ~andar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anþar~, from Proto-Germanic *~anþeraz~, from PIE *~h₂énteros~ ("other"). The PIE root *~h₂énteros~ is a comparative formation from *~h₂ent-~ ("front, forefront"), and its original sense was "the one opposite, the one facing" — i.e., the second of two — before broadening to "other." The semantic journey from "second" to "different" to "to change" completes in ~ändern~. Cognate with Hunsrik ~ennre~, English ~other~, Dutch ~ander~, Old Norse ~annarr~ (Swedish ~annan~, Danish ~anden~).
en.ärgern:
From Middle High German ~argern~ ("to worsen"), from Old High German ~argerōn~, derived from the adjective ~arg~ ("bad, wicked"). Cognate with English ~eerie~.

The adjective ~arg~ traces from MHG ~arc~, from OHG ~arg~, from Proto-West Germanic *~arg~, from Proto-Germanic *~argaz~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃erǵʰ-~ ("to copulate; ardent"). The semantic journey from "ardent, lustful" to "bad, wicked" reflects a moral judgment on excessive passion -- what was once merely "passionate" became "wicked" as Germanic Christianity imposed new values on old vocabulary. Cognates include Lithuanian ~eržùs~ ("ardent, stubborn") and Hittite ~arkari~ ("to copulate"). The modern German meaning of ~ärgern~ has softened considerably from "to make worse" to "to annoy, to irritate," and the reflexive ~sich ärgern~ ("to be annoyed") is among the most common expressions of everyday frustration. Dutch ~erg~ ("bad, severe") preserves the older adjective sense.
en.äußern:
From MHG ~ūzeren~ ("to bring out, express"), deadjectival from ~äußer~ ("outer, external"), itself the comparative of ~aus~ / ~außen~ ("out, outside"). ~Aus~ derives from MHG ~ūȥ~, from OHG ~ūȥ~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). A doublet of English ~out~; compare Dutch ~uit~, Low German ~ut~, Danish ~ud~.

The meaning of ~äußern~ is "to express, to utter (one's thoughts or feelings)" — to bring something inner to the outside. The cognate English verb ~utter~ (as in "to utter a word") followed the same semantic path from the same root: PGmc *~ūtizô~ (comparative of *~ūt~) yielded both German ~äußer~ and English ~outer~ / ~utter~. The physical image of moving speech outward from within is thus embedded in the very shape of the word.
en.üben:
From Middle High German ~üeben~, ~uoben~, from Old High German ~uoben~, from Proto-Germanic *~ōbijaną~ ("to do, practice"), the causative-iterative formation of a lost strong verb *~afaną~, from PIE *~h₃ep-~ ("to labor, work, toil"). The same PIE root gives Latin ~opus~ ("work") and ~opera~ ("effort, service") — whence English ~opera~, ~operate~, and ~opus~. Cognate with Dutch ~oefenen~ (with an ~n~-suffix extension), Old Saxon ~ōbian~, Old Norse *~œfa~ (Icelandic ~æfa~). The Swedish ~öva~ and Danish ~øve~ are borrowed from Middle Low German ~ôven~ rather than inherited.

The verb's core meaning, "to practice, to drill, to exercise," has remained remarkably stable across a thousand years of German. The reflexive ~sich üben in~ ("to practice at, to exercise in") preserves the iterative force of the original Proto-Germanic causative: not a one-time doing but repeated, deliberate effort. The derived noun ~Übung~ ("exercise, practice") and the adjective ~üblich~ ("usual, customary") both reflect this deep association between repeated action and established habit. German proverb: ~Übung macht den Meister~ ("Practice makes the master") — a direct calque of the Latin ~exercitium facit magistrum~.
